Her vocals were very secure, and her
dancing was charming.
Gill O'Brien was a force to be reckoned
with in the role of Aunt Ellen. No mellow
old woman here, but a wily, street-wise
matron, with a rambunctious sense of
humour and commanding voice and
presence,
and
frankly,
much
more
personality than we might normally expect
from Aunt Eller. I liked her, a lot.
Shane Byrne was a very credible and very
likeable Will Parker, with a good voice and
an even better sense of comedy. He was
well able to lead the Kansas City dance
and worked delightfully well alongside
Ado Annie.
Lynn
Carter
gave
a
petite,
perky,
powerhouse of a performance as Ado
Annie. Her acting and comedy were very
strong, but it was her facial expressions
that made her stand out, always beaming,
always mischievous and always alert. She
compelled the audience to take notice of
her. She also put so much energy and a
very fine voice into her musical numbers.
As the roguish, philandering peddler,
Ali Hakim, Paul Dicker relished the
opportunity to milk the comedy to the full,
and he did so with charm and character.
Only occasionally did he need to slow the
pace of his dialogue and emphasize his
comedic reactions, but this was a very
commendable performance.
Rory Dunne had a strong stature and a
good growly look for Jud Fry, which was
complemented by his strong acting and
delivery of lines, but without a shadow of
a doubt, his vocal delivery of Poor Jud
is Dead, and particularly Lonely Room,
was the musical highlight of the show.
The power, the tone and the quality of his
singing was awesome, so much so that I
almost wished him to win the knife fight
with Curly on the off-chance that he might
burst into song again. (No offence at all
to Curly!) A remarkably fine performance.
Hayley Campbell proved to be hilariously
obnoxious in the role of Gertie Cummings,
with a laugh that would put years on you.
A very nicely developed and performed
character.
Arthur McGauran provided gravitas and
excellent character comedy to the role of
Andrew Carnes, comfortably in control of
all his scenes, and a strong leader in The
Farmer and The Cowman.
As previously mentioned, there was
excellent and creative use of the chorus
throughout the show, particularly as
peripheral dressing to many of the
scenes. There were all business and well-
disciplined in the choreographed overture,
and if one or two of the tiny performers
didn't quite achieve their 'freezes', their
cuteness only added to the delight of
the audience. Vocally, the chorus were
excellent, with ever-consistent tone and
harmony. The Farmer and the Cowman
was vibrant and uplifting and the Oklahoma
Chorus was exquisite. The ladies in Out
of My Dreams and Many a New Day were
articulate and easy on the ear. Physically,
everyone gave 100% to their acting and
provided so much atmosphere to the box
social and to the auction scene. Dancing
throughout was precise, efficient and
gleefully performed.
There was very good attention to detail
in the costuming of the show, from head
to toe, with footwear being notably
appropriate at all times. I did wonder if
one or two of the hats on some of the
ladies were a bit more 'My Fair Lady' than
'Oklahoma!', but they were beautifully
made and presented. The ladies' dresses
were colourful and authentic, and the men
were well turned out. Ballet costumes
were attractive and in keeping with the
various moods of the piece, and I liked
the smartness of some of the men in
the wedding scene. Hair styles were
consistently good, as was make-up.
Visually, the show was very successful.
Sincere thanks to Dave Smyth in particular
and to all the front of house staff for their
courtesy and efficiency. It is always a
bonus to see the staff dressed for the
occasion. Dave, (who has always been a
bit of a cowboy!) looked wonderful, as did
the other cowboys and cowgirls.
The boots of the dynamic Mona Conroy
will be difficult to fill in future productions,
but as she retires from direction, she
leaves Naas with a legacy of excellence,
involvement and community pride that
will not be extinguished. While thanking
you all for a most enjoyable night of
entertainment in Naas, I wish you future
success in all your endeavours and I
would like to wish Mona a long and happy
retirement.

If anyone ever doubted the old saying 'the
apple doesn't fall far from the tree', they
should have seen the Muse production
of "Our House" where a new generation
of young thespians was led by a dynamic
couple who performed out of their skins
to make this a most memorable and
highly talented experience. Following
in the footsteps of their extremely
skilled and experienced parents, Conor
McNelis, as Joe Casey, and Julita Fox,
as Sarah, displayed talents that went far
beyond what one would expect, given
their tender years. They were quite
remarkable, and they were supported by
a cast that brimmed with talent, energy
and enthusiasm in every aspect of their
performances.
Director Martin McNellis really did his
homework to ensure that "Our House"
was as authentic to its era as possible,
and to stretch the talents of his young
principals to the max. In both of these
tasks, he succeeded most assuredly.
Furthermore, he stretched himself, taking
on a very modern piece with demanding
stage requirements. With a beautifully
crafted set, on a tight and unforgiving
stage, he achieved something of a
technical miracle. The 'Driving in my Car'
number, a combination of classy direction
and technical genius, was quite brilliant.
The staging of the show was clever,
concise, and ran like clockwork. The
design was excellent and the management
of all the moving pieces was a tribute not
only to the industrious stage manager,
Ted Germaine, but also to his team and
the cast members who worked together in
perfect harmony. The upper platform was
well used, especially for the presence of
the 'ghost' father, and props and furniture
were always authentic and moved in
and out efficiently. Astute direction also
contributed to perfectly timed costume
changes for the central character, which
played an essential role in the continuity
of the piece. Likewise, choreography
played an important role in the transitions,
highlighting
choreographer
Pamela
Glynn's astute appreciation of the drama
as much as the dance. She also perfectly
recreated
the
'Madness'
era,
with
wonderfully nostalgic and highly energetic
dance routines, which were performed
with dynamic enthusiasm and precision.
Lighting was an important part of the
drama, requiring very well-timed lightning
flashes at every transition. These were
achieved to perfection. The lighting
of ghostly Dad was delightfully cold
throughout, if once or twice, slightly too
dimly lit. The rest of the lighting plot was
colourful and atmospheric. Sound quality
was generally good, even if Dad was a
little under-amplified in the early scenes.
Between sound engineers and musical
director, a very careful balance was
maintained so that the hidden band never
overwhelmed the singers.
The ever youthful and dynamic Mary-Rose
McNally was the leader of that hidden band,
kept under-stage for the performance,
visible only to the cast by video-link, but
even from her darkened abode, she kept
a tight rein on the musical quality of the
show, with assured entrances and cut-
offs. She also produced balanced sound
and an astoundingly authentic 'Madness'
feel from her excellent musicians. So
much so that I initially wondered were
they using original backing tracks, but no,
they were just that good.
But the night belonged to the dynamism
that was abundantly evident on the stage.
Conor McNelis, as Joe, displayed a
level of maturity in his performance that
is uncommon for someone so young.
He understood his character and the
juxtapositions that he faced and played
both versions of himself with good
contrast and much intensity. His love for
Sarah was very well-delivered, and his
guilt and emotion in the final scenes was
spine-tinglingly sincere. Such a strong
and assured performance.
It was the equally mature, sensitive and
balanced performance from Julita Fox as
Sarah that made this central relationship
so powerful. Here is a young lady who
understands vulnerability and heartache
as convincingly as she displays the
confident and capable modern woman
who is prepared to go it alone when
required. Again, she handled the emotional
scenes with great sensitivity. Added to the
strong acting, both performers showed
excellent comedic timing and strong
vocals throughout.
As Dad, first time performer, Colm
McGuinness
showed
few
signs
of
nervousness,
giving
a
ghostly
performance that grew in intensity and
emotion as the show progressed. He is
also in possession of a fine set of vocal
chords.
Olivia Parkinson gave a warm and resolute
performance as Kath, Joe's widowed
mother. There was great strength in her
determination to survive her hardships
and great passion in her relationship with
Joe. Her songs were delivered with clarity
and sincerity.
Sally Fox as Billie, and Alanna Willets as
Angie provided the comedic back-up to
Sarah, and did so with a great sense of
fun, and often a caustic sense of humour.
These were strong performers who, given
that the show is very much a drama with
music, perhaps played just a little too
obviously to the audience rather than
to their fellow performers. They were,
nonetheless, delightfully funny and crass,
and both were very capable of belting
out their lyrics. On Joe's side of the table,
comedy support came from Cillian Fahy
as Emmo and Ciarán O'Keefe as Lewis.
Both made the most of their opportunities,
with Cillian in particular, acting out the
required immaturity to present himself as
the twit of the group.
As the bad apple, irresponsible delinquent
of the piece, Sean McInerney was a strong
and repugnant Reecey, as was required of
him. It's not always easy to play the bully,
but he did so with conviction.
There was a note-worthy performance
from old-timer, Aodan Fox, as the corrupt
businessman, Mr Pressman, and it's fair to
assume that the many younger performers
on the stage have learned a lot from his
self-assured, always considered and
highly professional approach to every part
he plays. Completing the younger cast
were good solid performances from Tara
Monaghan as Julie and Richard Germaine
as Callum, while Dara O'Callaghan, Ian
Collins, Laura O'Brien, Michelle Kelly,
Sarah Allen and Kim O'Dea filled a vast
array of supporting cameo roles with
credibility and confidence. A special
mention too, for the delightful cameo
performances of Cormac Ross as Elvis
and Cooper.
Sheer energy was the key to the success
of the chorus, whether it was the vocal
energy of their strong choral contributions,
or the physical energy of their wonderfully
performed dance routines. They were
never on stage looking lost or being
passive. They always contributed to the
atmosphere and ambiance of their scenes.
Visually,
the
show
was
also
most
successful. The black suit and white
track-suit of Joe worked brilliantly in
facilitating those numerous and essential
fast changes. Similarly, Sarah's costumes
were well selected to blend with each
scene.
Costumes
generally
were
attractive, era-appropriate and worn well
by the company. From hairstyles, to make
up, to footwear, the cast looked correct
from head to toe. The extra-speedy
on-stage costume change for Joe was
amazingly slick!
There's no such thing as a flawless or
perfect production, but it's an awesome
experience when a show comes close.
Not for the first time this season, I'm
feeling that awe. Well done, Muse, on
something pretty spectacular.

There was something nostalgic and
wonderful about seeing Director Ronan
Lardner and Musical Director, Shane
Farrell working side-by-side in the very
venue where they both cut their musical
teeth, under the guidance of the late, great
Joe O'Donoghue and the late, great Noel
Kirrane. How proud their past masters
would have been to see how both of their
students have established themselves
in musical theatre. They would most
certainly have been impressed with this
wonderfully joyful production of Sister Act.
Boasting a highly talented front line and
an energetic and enthusiastic chorus, this
was entertainment of the highest order.
An excellent comedian himself, director
Ronan Lardner managed to wring every
ounce of comedy out of the very funny
script, and added many little individual
touches, but he was just as thorough
about playing up the sentimental side of
the story.
The set for the show was as simple as
possible, given a stage that has no room
at all for massive pieces or storage, but
it was clean, effective and well-painted.
Only essential items of props and furniture
were apparent, and it was more than
enough. The centre piece of the set was an
excellent circular stained-glass window,
which, combined with really effective
lighting, looked superb. The confessional
boxes were very good, and the rest of the
props were appropriate and acceptable. A
centre stage black gauze was well used
both for isolating the forward scenes but
also as a bleed-through to create some
nice effects. Lighting was generally very
good, with atmospheric use of colours
and back light. Sound quality throughout
was just about perfect.
The band, under the direction of Shane
Farrell, obviously enjoyed every note of
this excellent musical score, playing with
a vibrant and precise energy, always on
point, and always sympathetic to the
vocalists on stage. Tempi throughout were
just perfect. Shane had gone to town on
the choral vocals, as evidenced by secure
harmonies, excellent diction and a certain
joie de vivre in performance. This was a
top drawer choral display. Musically and
physically, they performed out of their
skins, adding a secure backbone to the
whole production. Their sheer sense of
enjoyment was contagious.
Commanding the stage from the get-go,
Emma Brady proved to be the perfect
casting for the demanding role of Deloris
Van Cartier. Her acting and her comedy
were on point, her movement was fluid,
and when she sang… Wow! With a voice
like a finely tuned instrument, she raised
the roof in every number. Whether with
the gentle, dulcet and emotional tones
of 'Sister Act' or unleashing the inner
beast in 'Take Me to Heaven' and 'Raise
Your Voice', the vocal quality was simply
awesome. It almost converted me!
There was a sublime quality to the voice
and performance of Frieda McGrath as
the Mother Superior, dignity and decorum
epitomized, until the strain of coping
with Deloris eventually cracked her outer
shell. Then she delighted us with a very
funny and slightly demented rendition
of 'I Haven't Got A Prayer'. Frieda and
Emma played off each other absolutely
beautifully.
A young and endearing Alana Mullins
made a big impact as the shy and reserved
Sr Mary Robert, then floored us all with
her feisty power when she unleashed 'The
Life I Never Led'. Such talent from one so
young, and a very well-played role.
Who can resist a nun with attitude? With
a voice that could shatter concrete, a
presence that would ward of the devil, and
an abundance of comedic talent, Clodagh
Ruane rocked and rapped her way into
our hearts with a superb performance as
Sr Mary Lazarus.
Olivia McNama was filled with fun and
religious fervour as the highly animated
and extremely funny Sr Mary Patrick,
making the most of all her opportunities to
shine. There were equally accomplished
performances from Eimear McGovern as
Sr Mary Theresa and Sinead Whelan as Sr
Mary Martin-of-Tours.
Congratulations to the very talented
Declan Kelly for playing Monsignor O'Hara
with
great
empathy,
understanding,
excellent comedic timing and a modicum
of irreverent humour.
Norman Quinn presented us with a very
sweaty and very loveable Eddie, playing
the love-struck, weak-willed cop to
perfection. He realised his comedy most
effectively and sang like a nervous bird
until he found himself being suddenly
manly. A lovely performance.
Niall Conway was a strong and believable
gang-leader in the role of mafia-style
hoodlum,
Curtis.
His
stature
made
him imposing but it was his menacing
demeanour and his confident acting that
made him such a convincing character.
The man can sing a bit too. He was ably
assisted in his nefarious endeavours by
a trio of comically inept bad-guys, Stuart
Barrows as Joey, as smooth as he was
stylish, Thomas Edwards, as TJ, the
very funny idiot relation that everyone
denies knowing, and Michael Cooney,
the ludicrous Latino who represents the
strongest argument for tighter border
controls. Very good performances from
this whole team of desperados.
As Deloris's night-club sidekicks, Michelle
and Tina, Emer Kelly and Sinead Murphy
sang and danced delightfully and handled
their dialogue with assured comedic
ability. It's a pity these parts aren't bigger,
but very nicely played.
There was good support, too, from Sean
King as the 'disposable' Ernie, who also
doubled as an altar boy alongside Ruadhan
Gormally. Feargal MacMeanmain made a
delightful cameo appearance as the Pope,
even kneeling down to kiss the floor of the
school hall. A nice touch.
From a visual point of view, you can't
go too far wrong with nuns habits, and
in this case, they were worn well, and
increased delightfully in glitz and glamour
as the show progressed through to a
dazzling finale. Principal costumes were
all appropriate, although you could have
been a little more flamboyant with the
hoodlums outfits. Curtis was delightfully
dapper as the gang-leader. Eddie's triple
costume was very good, and not at all
obvious before he was disrobed. Wigs/
hairstyles were fine, although Deloris
might have had a slightly tidier corkscrew,
but it didn't impede the quality of her
performance. Make up seemed natural,
with no glaring eye-liners or polished nails
on the nuns. Good work.
Sister Act isn't the most challenging
show to stage or to perform, but it is
most certainly one of the best feel-good
shows of the modern era, and when it is
performed to such a high standard, it is
easy to get carried along by the euphoria
and the heavenly goodness of the piece.
This wasn't a very good production, it was
a very excellent production, and it was
a privilege to see Marian Choral Society
reaching such heights of achievement.
Thank you for a truly wonderful night.

Tralee's Siamsa Tíre is a beautiful venue,
and one that I always enjoy visiting, and
when the standard of production and
performance is as high as was presented
by LOST, it makes the journey south seem
somehow shorter and so worthwhile.
"Evita" is a wonderful biographical musical,
with a superb score and an intriguing
story, but it can be very demanding, which
makes the success of this production all
the sweeter. From sets and costumes
to
direction
and
choreography
and
magical musicianship, all the elements
came together beautifully to frame and
accentuate a cast of excellent performers.
Director
Grainne
O'Carroll's
passion
for this show was clearly evident in
her disciplined and beautifully stylised
production. The attention to detail was
excellent, from the eye-catching set to
the costumes, the lighting, the groupings
on stage and the right tone and mood of
each scene. With a very well-constructed
and painted set, featuring nice little
playing areas on the front aprons, and a
stunning Casa Rosada centrepiece, the
stage was beautifully and atmospherically
lit throughout, with good use of colours
and nicely defined special areas. Props
were generally very good, although I'd
like to have seen maybe more bunting
or national flags for the countries on the
Rainbow Tour. The projected footage of
the cinema, and then the newsreel of the
actual Eva Peron funeral was of very good
quality. The production was streamlined,
with little or no superfluous dressing or
action, which saw the focal point of the
action always clearly apparent, and it
helped to maintain a very good pace. If
she had felt so inclined, Grainne might
have added another dimension visually
by being a bit more flamboyant and
carnival minded in the costuming of the
'Buenos Aires' number. However, chorus
costumes had good variety between the
street people and the sophisticates, and
the men's uniforms were, by and large,
appropriate and well-worn. Eva Peron's
gowns were fabulous and flattering, her
red outfit being wonderful in allowing her
the freedom for the stylised dancing, and
the white balcony dress was exquisite.
Peron was sharp and elegant, and Che
was cool and casual.
Ranging from precise military style routines
to flamboyant street dances, including
very well-devised choreographed fights
and an elegant tango and waltz, a great
amount of thought and care went into
the work of choreographer, Tara Dore. It
was vibrant, fluent and mostly extremely
well executed by the chorus and dancers.
Dancing on chairs is never easy, but in the
'Art of the Possible' routine, the cast were
meticulously well-drilled. This was a most
varied and exciting dance show.
A very strong orchestra, under the
guidance and leadership of Musical
Director, Anna Connolly, played the
beautiful musical score with tone, balance
and wonderful expression. Rhythms and
pace were pretty much perfect. Chorus
Mistress, Caitriona Fitzmaurice, had her
singers well-drilled and full of expression
and articulation. The quality of the music,
throughout, was extremely high.
There can be few female roles as
demanding as that of Eva Peron, requiring
powerful vocals and a wide range of
emotions, and in Clodagh Harrington,
this production has found the perfect
performer for the role. From the flirtatious
social climber to the manipulative power
behind Peron, she infused her character
with style and dynamism, most often
expressed through a pitch perfect and
commanding
vocal
display.
Clodagh
played this role several years ago as a
very promising up-and-coming artiste,
but now she has come of age with a quite
brilliant performance.
There was a stirring performance too from
Marcus Nolan as Peron, strong in stature,
secure in his vocals, highly believable in his
acting and also fleet of foot as he fought
his way into power. This was a sincere and
well-rounded characterisation.
Sean McElligot, as the narrator, Che,
despite the annoyance of a dodgy radio-
mic for his early scenes, never lost his
composure and kept the story moving
with a strong and confident personality,
and an excellent voice.
Owen Rua Herlihy established himself as
the crooner Magaldi with a fine rendition
of 'On This Night of a Thousand Stars'.
Perhaps we needed to see more obviously
his flirting with Eva at the start, but his
frustration at her behaviour as the show
progressed was well-registered.
In the most thankless role of the Mistress,
Lauren Glennon did all you really can do,
which is to sell the beautiful 'Another
Suitcase in Another Hall' with conviction.
She displayed nice vocal quality and
expression.
All the cameo supporting roles, like
officers, ministers, sisters, servants and
townsfolk, were played with conviction,
and a special mention for little Kate
Roche, who was the delightful solo voice
in 'Santa Evita'.
If I was to be very critical, I could say that
one or two performers were a tad behind
the beat or stuttered in the execution of
some of their steps, but to be honest,
the overall impact of the very slick and
disciplined choreography washed away
any negative thoughts, as the chorus
and dancers gave 100% commitment
to every routine. They were vocally
extremely secure and their involvement in
the various scenes always had a purpose.
They were poignantly stiff and upright as
the pretentious Buenos Aires elite, and
strong and revolutionary as street people.
Very good work.
Giving that I attended this show on
opening night, I'm reluctant to be too
critical of minor technical issues, and I'm
prepared to believe that the glitches with
the radio-mics will be quickly eliminated.
Indeed, as the night progressed, it was
already being dealt with. However, the
sound quality was a little bit patchy and
uneven on occasions and did need some
attention.
No production achieves perfection, if such
a thing even exists, but when so many
aspects of a show reach such a high
level, it is fair to say that it was perfectly
stunning, as was most definitely the case
with this production. When the overall
effect is powerful enough to blur out the
small weaknesses, it says a lot about
talent and quality and sheer entertainment
value. This show was excellent. Thank
you for an amazing night and for your
hospitality and kindness.

Made in Dagenham, at its heart, is
a socially conscious, gritty dramatic
musical, peppered with good humour
to bring levity to often heart-breaking
situations. Its characters are strong and
well-written, and the central romantic
stories work hand in hand with the
strong commentary on social injustice.
It is, in many ways, as inspirational as it
is entertaining. On the dramatic level,
it works brilliantly, supported by an
ample hand-full of poignant laments and
anthems that make a powerful impact. It
certainly inspired a high-quality standard
of production and performance from
the dedicated cast of Kilmainham and
Inchicore, who delivered their goods with
conviction and no shortage of talent.
In the very safe hands of Director Art
McGauran, the potential of this piece was
fully realised, with good attention given to
aesthetically assimilating the settings and
the costumes to the era. On a set that was
appropriately industrial, good set pieces
were used to add colour and location,
while space was well used, even when
the stage was fairly full of bodies. My only
gripe with the technical presentation of
the show was over-amplification, which I
believe was the result of an over-exuberant
orchestra. A very confident and capable
band of players, under the leadership of
Musical Director, Barry Power, produced
quality accompaniment to the production,
albeit with a heavy handedness that, on
occasions, competed with the sung and
spoken words of a few characters on
stage. As a result, I felt that much of the
on-stage work was over-amplified to be
certain of being heard. No such problems
occurred, however, when the full chorus
let vent, with strong voices and precise
harmonies, indicating that they were
vocally very well prepared.
Lighting was varied and atmospheric,
with good use of pools of area lighting,
and the more vibrant show-biz numbers
were enhanced by an abundance of
colour and contrast. That industrial and
versatile stage was very well handled
and manipulated by a very industrious
stage crew, under the guidance of Stage
Manager, designer and builder, Colum
McDaid. With so many wonderful props
and furniture to negotiate, the scene
changes were surprisingly tidy and
efficient.
Siobhan Ryan put plenty of aggression
into the choreography of the shows torch-
songs, correlating the steps and body
language with the strength of the lyrics,
and making the numbers all the more
powerful. This was very good work. She
also provided energetic, showy routines
when the music demanded it, with style
and variety enhancing such numbers as
'Pay Day', 'This is America', 'Cortina!' and
'Viva Eastbourne'. She was also blessed
to have a company who gave 100% to
their movement.
Amy Penston played Rita O'Grady, the
reluctant hero of the story, with great
credibility
and
warmth.
There
was
sincerity in her heart-wrenching choices
between
motherly
responsibility
and
being a pioneer of social change, and
she handled the conflict with her husband
with a touching balance of love and
exasperation. She also played the lighter
side of her character with good comedic
awareness, and when she opened up her
vocal chords, she excelled.
As her husband Eddie, Gavin Molony was
warm and affectionate in the home and
delightfully roguish as one of the lads in
his place of work, but it was during the
conflicted scenes with his wife, and in his
final realization of her true worth that his
talents as an actor really shone through. A
compassionate and moving performance.
His singing was also remarkably good.
The O'Grady children, Megan Lynch as
Sharon and Evan Roberts as Graham, did
all that was required of them, and played
their emotional scenes particularly well.
Very nice work.
Yvonne McCarthy was a strong and robust
Connie Riley as the part required, yet she
portrayed her more vulnerable self, and
indeed her faded self in hospital, with
dignity and sincerity. This was a lovely
warm performance, and 'Same Old Story'
was very well delivered. Sean Hendley, as
Monty, gave a great and often comedic
character to the ineffectual and easily
rebuffed rep of his female workers. But it
was the moment when he heart-breakingly
declared his love for the departed Connie
that we saw his acting at its finest. I don't
believe there were many dry eyes in the
theatre. Beautifully performed.
The most appalling string of expletives
rolled naturally off the tongue of Sophia
Daly, in a deliciously crass and amusing
performance as potty-mouthed Beryl.
What does it say about us, as an
audience, that the utterance of the 'F'
word can reduce us to fits of hysterical
laughter? Well, perhaps it was the perfect,
often caustic, delivery of the word from
a very accomplished character actress/
comedienne that made it work so well
without offending.
Lisa Younge, as Cass, Nikki Johnston
as the addled-brained Clare and Louise
O'Connor as the flighty glamour girl
Sandra all added strong characterisations
to
the
Dagenham
workforce
and
performed with energy and commitment.
Brian Carroll played Harold Wilson very
much as a caricature of the famous
Prime Minister, making him both crass
and likeable all at once. This was a
good comedy performance with a well-
delivered rendition of 'Always A Problem'.
It takes a powerhouse of a performer
to play the powerhouse of a politician
that was Barbara Castle, and there was
no better a woman for the task than
Naoimh Penston, who looked and acted
the character with great reality, although
I doubt if the real Barbara had a set of
lungs like Naoimh, whose 'Ideal World'
deservedly raised the roof. A brilliant vocal
performance. David Supple proved to be
a delightfully pompous, upper-class twit
in the role of executive, Jeremy Hopkins,
even if he was upstaged and out-smarted
by his equally convincing and dignified
wife, Lisa, beautifully played by Vanessa
Murphy. Rogue of the story, American
chief executive, Mr. Tooley, was played
with unrestrained unpleasantness by the
very capable Terry Martin, who was also
well up to the vocal demands of 'This is
America'. Good vocals, and an amusing
cheesiness, were also presented by Kevin
Macken-Tierney as the Cortina Man. Jack
Halpin as Ron Macey and Darragh Carroll
as Gregory Hubble added good comedy
and character to their management roles,
and Brian Dennison as Stan competently
led an accomplished team of lads at
the Ford Factory. A veritable myriad of
supporting roles were all played with
conviction by a cast who worked very well
together as a team.
When they opened up in their anthems,
the chorus made a powerful vocal
contribution to the show, and their
physical presence was highlighted by
precise dance and movement and good
acting and reacting to the circumstances
in which they found themselves. Again,
the team effort was very focused, strongly
delivered and appreciated.
Wigs and hairstyles were notably excellent
throughout the show, and costumes were
perfect, from work overalls down to casual
daywear. Nothing looked out of place.
Outfits for This is America and Cortina
added a smattering of razzle-dazzle to the
proceedings. Make-up looked appropriate
and natural, and an excellent job was
done on visually realising the sickness of
the ailing Connie.
With a company so secure in their
characterisations,
and
a
production
team that high-lighted both the comedy
and the poignant drama of the piece,
I'm delighted that my first experience of
Made in Dagenham was in such safe and
talented hands. Thank you sincerely for
such an enjoyable and worthwhile musical
experience.

For audiences who have been starved
of live theatre throughout the Covid
pandemic, this was exactly the kind of
comedy-driven, rib-tickling, finger-clicking
entertainment that was required to warm
their hearts and to lift their spirits. 'All
Shook Up', possibly the best of the juke-
box musicals, is all about comedy and
fun, coupled with the ever-popular hits of
the late, great Elvis, and an appreciative
Fermoy audience enjoyed every minute of
it.
In the safe hands of director Valerie
O'Leary, this was a production that
cruised along at a good pace throughout.
There was good definition of characters,
and good emphasis on the comedy
of the piece, both the verbal and the
physical, and for those musical numbers
that weren't dominated by dance, good
pictures were painted on the stage. A
somewhat abstract set, at first sight,
proved
to
be
both
functional
and
adaptable, with well selected set pieces
and furniture helping to create the various
scenes. The added fairground silhouette
on the back wall completely changed
the look of the set for act two. Scene
changes, under the guidance of Stage
Manager, Jacqui Creed, were smooth and
sufficiently speedy as to not interrupt the
flow of the show. The motorbike, the petrol
pump, the juke-box were among the very
good props. Lighting was generally very
impressive, with particularly good back
lighting and very good transitions from
state to state. The sound was so good
that I didn't even really notice it, except
the few sound effects, which were good
and well timed. All in all, this was a show
that seemed effortless technically, due to
well-directed efficiency. Very nice work.
Niamh
Twomey's
choreography
was
vibrant and varied and added so much to
the overall production. Some of the more
energetic routines tested her dancers
and chorus, who managed to achieve a
high level of proficiency, with the ladies
generally outshining the men, but no-
one was lacking in energy or enthusiasm.
Niamh also injected good comedy into
many of the routines, particularly 'Teddy
Bear/Hound Dog', 'Let Yourself Go' and
'You're the Devil in Disguise'.
Between them, Musical Directors Robbie
Pender and Deirdre Foley presented
a good well-balanced sound from the
orchestra pit and some very accomplished
choral singing from the folks on-stage.
'Heartbreak Hotel', 'Can't Help Falling
in Love' and 'If I Can Dream' were
particularly vocally inspiring. Both chorus
and principals seemed well-rehearsed in
their music, and the overall quality of the
music was very good indeed. Rhythms
and tempi were secure throughout.
Michael-Anthony
Greene
was
an
energetic, hip-swivelling, and extremely
cool Chad who seemed to thoroughly
enjoy his role. His singing was very suited
to the rock'n'roll genre, and his ballads
were nicely handled. He also had a fine
sense of comedy.
More than a match for him was Alison
McCormack's Natalie, who was fiery
and feisty when required to be, but also
delightfully vulnerable and insecure. She
played her assumed character Ed with
very good comedy. Vocally she was very
confident throughout.
Michelle Smith gave a very good
performance in the role of Sylvia, striking a
good balance between concerned mother,
lethargic café owner and empathetic friend
and love-interest of Jim. She achieved all
of these with good humour and with a
most pleasant singing voice.
Rory Ward played Dennis the nerd with a
wonderful sense of nerdiness and fun and
easily won over the audience with great
vocal and physical comedy. This was a
most assured performance from a very
fine character comedian, who also knows
how to sell a song.
Equally assured and competent was
Colette Daly as the feisty vamp Miss
Sandra.
She
handled
Chad
with
dismissive authority and made the most of
her comical love for Ed and did it all with
impressive vocal quality.
Jack Fitzgerald gave some fancy footwork
and a remarkably fine voice to his
characterisation of Dean and played the
pampered mummy's boy to a tee. This
was a good comedy performance, with
believable romantic notions for Lorraine,
who was played most convincingly be
Michelle Cooke. Here is another vibrant
young performer who made a fine job of
her singing, her comedy and her romance.
Rebecca Beausang maintained a strong
and comedic sense of authority as Mayor
Matilda Hyde, and then melted delightfully
under the amorous attentions of Diarmuid
AIMS National President Rob Donnelly
with Michael Greene  (Chad) and Ali
McCormack (Natalie)
Vaughan's Sheriff Earl. The timing between
these two was very good, and Diarmuid
managed to speak volumes with his body
language. When he eventually got to
speak, he won over his woman with self-
assured authority and very good comedy.
Good acting and vocal support came from
Lisa Feerick as Henrietta, Orla O'Dwyer as
Amorous, Hugh Mulqueen as Brad, and
Stephen Niland impressed as the prison
warden and the bus driver.
Energy and enthusiasm were the order of
the day from a chorus who sang very well,
acted their socks off and danced with a
good degree of competence. Some of the
dancers were better than others, but no-
one let themselves down, and the overall
contribution of the chorus to the show
was of a very good standard.
Costume-wise, all was proper and correct,
with good prison outfits at the start,
colourful yet not over-glamorous outfits
for the townsfolk, and then deliciously
over-the-top fantasy costumes for Devil
in Disguise. Make-up was generally good,
but Natalie's stubble when she became Ed
could have been a bit more pronounced.
From where I sat, it wasn't too noticeable.
The ladies all had hairstyles appropriate to
the era, and the men were well-groomed.
The Front of House display for this show
was absolutely brilliant, with a highly
appropriately decorated foyer, featuring a
'Tunnel of Love', memorabilia about Elvis,
bunting everywhere, and so much more,
all related to the show. Excellent and
enjoyable work, combined by a friendly
and informative front of house staff.
Musically, this show hit all the right
notes, while visually and technically, it
was colourful and slick. Performances
were universally of a high order and the
company on stage seemed to enjoy
themselves as much as the audience did.
That kind of feel-good is infectious, and
Fermoy Musical Society produced it in
bucket-loads. Congratulations to all and
thank you for the fun.

A very fine sense of musicality was my
first impression of this production, led by a
delightfully mellow and tuneful orchestra,
comprised of very capable soloists,
particularly the violin and the woodwind.
Musical
Director/Conductor,
Jimmy
Brockie, did an excellent job, leading from
the piano. The quality, tone and volume
of the music was always extremely good,
and he gave good leadership to the on-
stage performers too. The three credited
Chorus Mistresses, Lorraine Crowley,
Denise Crowley and Aoibheann Carey-
Philpott, should all be very pleased by the
strong vocal performances of the chorus
and the children.
Director,
Jacinta
McBride's
greatest
achievement with this production was to
cast two completely inexperienced leads
and to ensure that they reached a level of
confidence and ability to carry the show
so successfully. Inspirational leadership
is a great quality in a director. There was
no question that she put much thought
into every aspect of the performance,
from good use of the available space
to the fine discipline of the Von Trapp
children. The only area which possibly
needed a bit more attention was the
pace of the dialogue, which on several
occasions was hampered by overly-long
dramatic pauses. But most commendable
was the performances she drew out of
the delightfully natural and competent
children. This was very good work.
Technically, I always appreciate when a
company makes good use of very limited
facilities, as was the case here. A great
piece of work was done on creating the
Von Trapp mansion with a nice white
staircase and dome topped pillars and
an attractive set of French doors with a
pleasing mountainous back piece. Almost
as good was the quickly erected pillars
and railings for the convent cemetery.
Less successful was the black curtains
used for the convent, with 2 rather small
and tawdry stained-glass windows. It
was enough to suggest the location, but
a bit of tidier artwork could have made it
much more substantial. I commend the
stage crew for keeping things moving at
a good pace, and for managing the good
selection of props and furniture. The only
scene change that didn't really work was
going from the terrace back into the house
interior which occurred while "No Way To
Stop It" was ongoing, and necessitated
the principals leaving the stage while they
were still singing.
Lighting throughout was very satisfactory,
even if one or two black-outs seemed to
happen slightly early. Sound quality was
impressive, and well-balanced with the
band.
In a show that doesn't demand too much
from a choreographer, Chloe O'Leary
managed to make her mark with good
and varied routines for the children,
and a particularly nicely choreographed
'Landler' for Maria and the Captain, which
they performed very well.
Playing her first leading role, Maeve
Murphy was very impressive as Maria. Her
relationship with the Von Trapp children
was warm and endearing and she handled
her realisation of being in love with the
Captain very nicely. She possessed a
most pleasant singing voice, and her
only flaw, musically, was to occasionally
be slightly behind the beat, causing the
MD to pull back the orchestra. This was,
however, a very commendable first lead.
Likewise, Robert J. Cogan was on his first
theatrical outing as Captain Von Trapp.
He had very good stature and presence,
and delivered his lines very well, and he
proved, in 'Edelweiss', to have a very
pleasant singing voice. One wonders why
he took so long to become involved in
musical theatre, and I predict that he will
play many roles in the future as he grows
in confidence.
Angela Tanner was a gentle and motherly
Mother Abbess, firm but compassionate
in her dealings with Maria and the other
nuns. She gave a fine rendition of 'Climb
Every Mountain'.
There was more than a hint of Groucho
Marx about Glen Barton in the role of
Uncle Max, not only in appearance
but also in his comedic antics. He was
a firm favourite with the audience,
and while I found his interpretation of
the character a tad pantomimic for a
minister for culture, it was an enjoyable
and
well-sustained
characterisation.
Lorna Hughes brought a good level of
elegance to Baroness Elsa, yet she was
delightfully catty in her encounters with
Maria, very nicely realising the comedic
element of her nature. Both she and Max
performed well in their musical numbers.
As Liesl, Clodagh Tanner performed very
comfortably and set a fine example for
her junior siblings, showing confidence
and understanding of her character. She
looked well, alongside Fionn Mehigan
in the role of Rolf, who was a believable
suitor, and transformed competently into
a misguided and confused Nazi. Both
made a very good job of 'Sixteen Going
on Seventeen'.
All of the Von Trapp children were
delightful and very well disciplined. Andrei
Macanovic was a charming Kurt, and
Aidan Crowley was a good typical boy
about to become a man. Orla Noonan
was a cute and enchanting little Gretl, Lexi
Costin's Marta was quirky and inquisitive,
Ella Hughes Curtin was deliciously roguish
as Louisa and most impressive was the
clever clogs Brigitta, perfectly portrayed
by Róisin Noonan.
Olive Vaughan was a very believable
harassed
house-keeper,
and
Fred
Ryan Spengeman was a credible butler
turned Nazi. Sisters Berthe, Sophia and
Margaretta, as played by Liz Hesse-
O'Sullivan, Mairead Hayes and Ava
Crowley Costin respectively, gave a
tuneful rendition of 'How Do You Solve
a Problem', and more impressively, they
managed to be very individual in creating
their characters. Herr Zeller was as
vicious as a rottweiller and impressively
obnoxious, as played by a very capable
Jerry Fitzgerald. There was good support,
too, from Kevin O'Keeffe, doubling
as Admiral Von Schreiber and Baron
Elberfeld, Mary O'Flynn as Baroness
Elberfeld, Marian O'Mahony as Frau Zeller
and Aimee Manning as Ursula. Betty
Brosnan, who greeted me so delightfully
in Front of House, made a very worthwhile
cameo appearance as the runner-up in
the Kaltzberg Festival.
The evening got off to a wonderful start
with a beautifully tuneful and articulate
Nuns Chorus, led by Lorna Hughes as
the soloist. Indeed, throughout the show,
these ladies gave an excellent exhibition
of choral singing. They were also very well
turned out, and principals were always
appropriately
attired.
The
children's
costumes were neat and tidily worn. Good
work here from the wardrobe team, and
make up throughout looked completely
natural.
The community spirit of this group is so
strong and obviously the key to creating
a wonderful atmosphere in the hall, and it
filtered through to myself and the whole
audience. My most sincere thanks for your
warm hospitality, and for a most enjoyable
performance of a show that I love dearly.

BOSCO captured the atmosphere of
Halloween from the get-go with their
production of 'The Addams Family',
introducing us to the weirdest of weird
families, and their deceased ancestors, in
a vibrant and engaging opening chorus,
played against an attractively eerie set.
The main structure of the set was well-
conceived and nicely painted, and props
and furniture throughout were nicely
made, or acquired. The torture "chair" was
impressively dangerous, and Pugsley's
rack was a thoughtful creepy piece of
punishment apparatus. The representation
of the moon was well-achieved, but not
particularly magical, even if the scene
was nicely played. Lighting was generally
at a good level, with all the action clearly
visible, and there were some nice effects
using gobos, although they were perhaps
a little over-used. Spotlights were well
directed, and effects, (lightening, etc.)
were very satisfactory. Sound quality was
good throughout, with good cueing and
good balance. Stage managers, Olivia
Pentony and Maria Rafferty, assisted by an
industrious stage team, had many pieces
of furniture to move, and worked hard to
achieve good variation in the settings,
but the often lengthy scene changes,
sometimes with musical accompaniment,
but sometimes with silence, did affect the
flow of the action.  While directors Corinna
McCaughey and Jim McGuigan presented
us with a good, polished production, I did
feel that visually, the comedy of the piece
could have been more exaggerated.
In the role of Gomez, Kyle Emerson was
a suitably authoritative figure, except, of
course, when confronted by his wife. Kyle
managed to convey both his love and his
fear of Morticia convincingly and he had
the vocal quality required for the role. I
did feel that on occasions he could have
played his comedy with a greater sense of
the ridiculous, but this was, nevertheless,
a good portrayal. As Morticia, Lauren
Galway was deliciously vampish and
I'm not surprised she frightened the wits
out of Gomez. She had a pleasant and
confident voice and played the cold-
blooded matron to a tee.
Anna-Maria
Boyle's
Wednesday
maintained
a
convincing
dead-pan
expression for most of the show, which
worked perfectly in highlighting her
weirdness. Her singing was very good,
with 'Pulled' being a high point of
musicality. Her relationship with Lucas
was also very believable.
Nicole McCann-Finegan made a strong
impression in the role of Pugsley, playing
her comedy very well and singing
delightfully. Daryll Galloghly was a very
alternative Fester, playing him with a kind
of impish sense of mischief, and it worked
extremely well. He was very capable as
a comedian, and used his physicality to
gain additional laughs. A genuinely funny
performance.
Grandma Addams was disgusting, and
brilliant all at once, played so adeptly by
Anne-Marie McAleenan, who squeezed
every last drop of comedy out of her
character. Of all the stage  characters, she
was perhaps the one who best captured
the exaggerated essence of the story.
Brian Leavy was a suitably dull spirited
Lurch, if a tad too young for the role, but
he performed with confidence. Shane
O'Keefe was a spirited Lucas Beineke
and played extremely well opposite
Wednesday. He got both the gormless
and the determined sides of the character
just right. As the straight-laced father,
Mal, Damien Lavery was suitably austere
and enjoyed lightening up when he
discovered his old self, much as Helena
Hughes achieved the transition from
nervous, dissatisfied wife to hot-blooded
vamp in the role of Alice. Her Waiting was
competently performed, although both
she and Mal seemed less secure in the
difficult 'Crazier Than You' quartet.
It was a lovely touch to introduce "Young
Wednesday" into Gomez's memories
during 'Happy/Sad', and Aoife Jennings
performed it beautifully.
Ann Marie Morgan's choreography was
varied, energetic and always appropriate
to the scene. There was good use of
talented acrobats and ballet dancers
which keep everything interesting and
engaging. As befitted the nature of the
show, there was a good comedic, surreal
feel to her numbers. I wasn't overly
impressed with the impact of The Moon
and Me, but did appreciate the novelty
of its choreography. Overall, the dancing
was uplifting and made a very positive
impact on the production. The pace of
the show, apart from the lengthy scene
changes, was good, but I did feel that had
the production gone for the same level of
outrage that the choreography achieved,
it would have been more comical.
Good in their appearance, good in their
dancing and movement and good in their
vocal contribution to the show, the chorus
and dancers worked hard all night. There
were one or two stand out dancers, but
everyone made a good impression.
Hats off  to the cast and the wardrobe team
who, between them, came up with a very
original and impressive set of costumes.
All of the principals looked impressive and
in-character, while the ghostly ancestors
were a fabulous spectacle. Wigs were
equally impressive and make-up was
weird and wonderful. Visually, the whole
piece had a lovely feeling of Halloween.
Well done.
Very much thrown in to the position of
Musical Director at the eleventh hour,
Elizabeth Freeburn acquitted herself very
respectably, keeping good control of the
small band. There were perhaps a few
occasions when the chorus had too much
free rein with cut-offs, and 'Crazier Than
You' seemed to give a few problems to
the singers, but in general, the show was
musically sound, and well balanced.
Even with the usual heightened sense of
community involvement and high spirits, I
did feel that perhaps the production team
needed to throw caution a little more to
the wind and present this show with an
even greater sense of the ridiculous. It was
there, particularly in the choreography, and
even at the level at which it was pitched,
it proved to be a most enjoyable theatrical
experience. Thank you to all involved for
your dedication and enthusiasm, and
sincere thanks to Jim McGuigan and the
front of house team for the wonderful
hospitality and refreshments.

Revenge of the Nostalgist
UCD Musical Society has been around
for some time and usually produce quirky
works like 'Urinetown' or 'The 25th Annual
Putnam County Spelling Bee' or they
revive a Sondheim or a Kander & Ebb with
a knowing and somewhat revisionist slant
and a fierce originality. So, it was a bit of
a surprise when they chose Dolly Parton's
hit show '9 to 5' as their first musical this
season. I mean there's not a lot a director
can do with it apart from follow what the
countless other versions out there do and
create a feel-good romp. Bearing in mind
the New York Times described it in 2009
as "an overinflated whoopee cushion"
and a "gaudy, empty musical", so it is a
bit of a challenge to make it work in 2022,
given the rise of the #metoo movement
and so on! Anyway, I went along with an
optimistic curiosity to see UCD's take on
this classic nostalgic crowd-pleaser.
UCD Astra Hall is not really a theatre in
the traditional sense in that it doesn't have
flying or tabs or a platform stage. It's a
general-purpose auditorium, often used
for lectures and gigs and the occasional
play or musical. We could see the set on
entry, and it was a wide representation of
a 'modern' office, complete with upstage
windows and the doors of an elevator. It
was quite impressive in its detail, more
like a TV studio set or a film set. There
was a wooden framed bed at centre
stage, which looked out of place, and I
thought maybe they work them so hard
that the boss makes them sleep there! But
no, it was set for the first number, "9 to
5", where the ensemble went through the
motions of waking up, dressing etc. and
going to work.
It started very well, great harmonies on
the title song by chorus mistress Ava
Barry and super big sound from the large
orchestra expertly driven by Amber Dixon,
with nice tight choreography by Niamh
O'Brien of a large energetic ensemble.
We eventually arrived at the office proper,
complete with desks etc. Here we met
the three female leads; Violet Newstead
played by Jennifer Byrne, Doralee Rhodes
(basically Dolly Parton) played by Lia
Mullan and Judy Bernly played by Chloe
Burke. The whole plot is about how they
try to change the hearts and minds of big
business and destroy misogyny.
Ms Byrne played widowed Violet as quite
high-status, fuming over not getting
promoted,
when
she
believed
she
deserved it. Her singing was very good,
particularly on "Around Here" and with
Joe on "Let Love Grow" and on "One of
the Boys" she excelled both vocally and
in the dance. Violet introduced newbie,
Judy, around the office and took her
under her wing. Chloe Burke who played
Judy, a mousey and embittered stay-at-
home wife thrust into the big bad world by
her ex-husband, had this haunting PTSD-
like quality to her performance which
really worked here. Judy is usually played
as a comic relief character, but Ms Burke
didn't push the comedy at all. It was still
there, but it was more like pathos than
farce. Her voice was stunning on "Get
Out and Stay Out" the big power ballad
of the show and she mapped Judy's
journey from mouse to lion with skill. The
final character of the trio was Doralee,
who was the boss's secretary. Lia Mullan
played the misunderstood Texan with a
'homespun' freshness that was enjoyable
to watch. Wrongly accused of being
the boss's mistress, she set the record
straight and joined the other two on a
quest to serve him his just desserts. Ms
Mullan had a good grasp of the Country
& Western genre that most of her songs
were written in, and she had a cheekiness
that enlivened the character.
All three had their own reasons for
hating the boss, Franklin J Hart Jr, here
played by Gearoid Riordan. Mr Riordan
had the unenviable task of portraying a
despicable, chauvinistic misogynist. But
he did it well! His singing was on point,
especially on "Here for You", where he
graphically fantasised about seducing
Doralee. His wife Missy, clearly oblivious
to his philandering ways, was played by
a fur-clad Aoife Blake, who in this version
became gay by the end of the show.
Hart's office manager, Roz Keith - in a
brilliant performance by Alice Morgan,
was obsessively in love with him. Ms
Morgan captured the character of the
repressed, nerdish fantasist perfectly. Her
song, "Heart to Hart" had the audience
whooping with joy and her second song,
the sad "5 to 9" had them in the palm of
her hand. Lovely, nuanced performance
from Ms Morgan.
These were the principal roles in the show,
and they were well cast I believe, and
each performer was quite good. However,
there was a disconnect between the
characters here. They didn't blend. There
was very little dynamism between Violet,
Doralee and Judy - we didn't believe that
they were united. Hart and Roz did have
a good chemistry and worked well the
couple of times they were on together.
But the three amigos didn't really gel for
me. It didn't help that the scene changes
and transitions took so long, thus ruining
the pace and the lighting was badly
miscued and the sound was patchy. I'm
sure stage managers, Clodagh Cullen and
Aoife O'Sullivan speeded things up during
the run, but the real problem was not
them, they had to deal with an unwieldy
set, which was clearly not designed for
theatre.
Directors, yes there were two, Michael
Bergin and Cormac Gilligan, seemed to
pay very little attention to detail both in
the set and in some of the performer's
actions, which made the production seem
quite ill-thought-out. For example: when
they tied up Hart in the office, they didn't
actually tie him up - they just draped the
cord around him, so his lines about being
unable to move were met with giggles
from the audience; similarly, when they
placed him on the bed, they just draped
the rope around his neck and didn't tie
him to the bed, yet this is referred to in the
book. We could see the stagehand in the
'photocopy' machine feeding the A4 paper
through the slot; there was nothing written
on the paper on Joe's clipboard but yet it's
referred to by Violet and Joe; when Violet
was 'fixing' the garage opener, she didn't
actually do anything to it; no liquid in cups
or kettle; the size of the 'corpse' on the
hospital trolley was too small - I could go
on with many more examples, but this is
what I mean about lack of attention to
details. Details matter as you are asking
your audience to suspend their disbelief
and they want to, and the details help
the illusion and our engagement with the
production. I believe that details also help
the performer believe in their character
and their actions.
Anyway, back to the performers. In a
rather underwritten role, Joe was the
nerdy junior accountant who fell for Violet.
Played by Patrick Mac Fhionnlaoich, he
made the most of the role and his song
with Violet "Let Love Grow" was quite
sweet. The office lush, Margaret, was a
great role to get the teeth into, and Alice
O'Loughlin Kennedy did just that! She
didn't go over the top with the drunk act,
which was the right decision, choosing to
play her as mildly inebriated. The reveal
at the end of the show, where she has
sobered up, was very well done. The
CEO of the organisation, Mr Tinsworthy,
was played by Alan Markey, he oozed
that CEO confidence and his exchange
with Violet towards the end of the show
was rather good. Other roles of note were
Violet's son Josh, well played by Eoin
Ó'Dúinín; Doralee's husband Dwayne
also well played by Luke Byrne, complete
with Texan drawl and Judy's oily ex, Dick,
played with simpering misogyny by Owen
Finnegan. It should be said that I enjoyed
the energy of the entire cast on this show,
they played it for all they were worth,
especially the ensemble. What they lacked
in direction I feel they more than made up
for with liveliness, due in no small part to
the choreographer and chorus mistress.
It struck me as I was watching the show
that it didn't seem to have benefitted
from much rehearsal, which may have
explained the holes. Whilst the performers
were
clearly
well-rehearsed
in
the
choreography and the music/singing, lack
of acting rehearsals may have accounted
for some of the problems I saw in the
performers. It also appeared to have been
somewhat busked in terms of set moving
and lighting and sound operation, possibly
indicating few technical rehearsals.
As I mentioned at the start, UCD are
renowned for presenting quirky, off-beat
entertaining
and
imaginative
shows.
Sadly, this was not one of them.

Family Plot
Staged in the National Opera House in
Wexford for just four performances in
late November and early December, this
show produced by Oyster Lane Theatre
Group was fast and furious with wonderful
orchestrations by Patrick Clancy and slick
choreography by Jonny Smith all held
together by director Thomas O'Leary. His
interpretation, whilst not adding anything
new, was solid and there were some stand
out moments of theatre where everything
just came together. He was blessed with
a few excellent performers who added
their own idiosyncratic takes on their
characters which the director wisely left
in.
It ran very smoothly and whilst it looked
good at times, the set, by Mark Redmond
didn't work for me and some of the
lighting states failed to light the actors. It
started with a very low energy, but when
the Ancestors entered, it picked up and
didn't let up until the end. This was helped
by Stage Manager Colin Murphy, who
kept the scene changes smooth.
And so, to the actors: the success of
this show depends on the character of
Gomez to keep the energy going, so it
is imperative that the performer playing
Ruth Donegan's kooky Grandma Addams
scares the daylights out of Ami Stahlut's
Alice Beineke
him has energy, charm, wit and above
all else excellent comic timing. The
director wisely chose long time member
Neal O'Leary to play Gomez. Mr O'Leary
had superb comic timing in this role. He
created a kind-hearted but very weird
Gomez, which is exactly how he should
be played. Gomez isn't normal and many
actors seem to forget this, but Mr O'Leary
didn't. He had a Robin Williams quickness
and timing mixed with early Steve Martin
and Peter Sellers mannerisms to create
a brilliant character. His singing was
good, going for expression rather than
vocal dexterity. His scenes with Morticia
and Wednesday really convinced and he
delivered "Happy/Sad" with a gorgeous
emotional intensity. Morticia was played
with a haughty imperiousness by Niamh
Bolger.
She had this lovely vibrato in her voice,
which gave a new resonance to Morticia's
songs particularly "Just Around the
Corner" and "Secrets" with Alice. Her
characterisation of Morticia was super,
physically quite domineering with a biting
sarcasm yet quite maternal to Pugsley.
She played the rivalry with Wednesday
with a quiet sub-text and had a great
dynamic with Gomez. They bounced off
each other very well.
Niamh
Cullen's
Wednesday
was
a
petulant, spoilt teenager used to getting
her own way and she oozed danger. Her
singing was first-rate, the highlight for me
being "Crazier Than You" with Lucas and
"Pulled" where she really showed off her
range. A very good performance. Playing
her Uncle Fester was Michael O'Gorman
who had great energy in the role. He leapt
around the stage with the ancestors like
he was possessed. His asides and direct
address to the audience was spot-on and
his singing was very good especially on
"The Moon and Me", which was staged
beautifully. Her brother Pugsley was
played by the young Sam Bolger, who
absolutely nailed Pugsley's character. He
was cheeky, precocious, and quite evil
at times. His dead-eyed stare was very
effective, and he sang "What If" with a
lovely emotion. Playing his Grandma was
Ruth Donegan with a cackle and a hiss
and a mad hairdo and very heavy make-
up.
Her voice was great, she had just the
right amount of rasp and her slowness
worked well. She was very funny in "Full
Disclosure" and had a nice dynamic with
Pugsley. The family butler, Lurch, was
played by Seán Hendley in a masterclass
of physical comedy. His pace throughout
the show never wavered and in the dance
numbers he was always a step behind as
he should be.
Excellent timing and a glum demeanour
made him one of the funniest characters
on stage.
The plot is all about Wednesday falling in
love with a 'normal' person, Lucas, getting
engaged and inviting him and his family
over to hers for dinner so that they can tell
the folks. Lucas Beineke, the all-American
boy-next-door type, was played by
Thomas Furlong. At first glance, he's the
last person you would think Wednesday
would be interested in. Or indeed that he
would fall for her as she's so dour and
pessimistic, but they did fall in love and
that's the main plot of the whole show.
Their incompatibility. Mr Furlong played
him with a lovely energy and a sort of
innocence that worked. His singing on
"Crazier Than You" with Wednesday
was excellent and they sounded great
together. Accompanied by his parents,
Alice and Mal, who were played by Ami
Stahlut and Brian Kelly, he shows up for
dinner. Ami Stahlut had an amazing voice,
and she sang "Waiting" with such energy
and feeling and emotion that the audience
erupted into unrestrained applause and
cheering. Her portrayal of Alice was just
right, the stay-at-home wife and mother
who wants to feel wanted again, wants
to matter. Mal is a great role show as the
character has a very recognisable journey;
from stuffy accountant to ageing rocker.
Brian Kelly did this very well, initially he
portrayed Mal as an uptight ordinary guy
appalled at Gomez and his family. But
when he believed that he might lose Alice,
he found his inner hippy.
Anyway, as you can imagine things don't
go according to plan, but it all ended up
unhappily ever after as they wouldn't
have wanted it any other way. The show
featured some marvellous set pieces such
as the whole "Moon and Me" sequence,
which was beautifully choreographed
and lit, topped off with Greg O'Leary's
descending moon projections. There
was also a swing which was flown in for
Gomez and Wednesday's "Happy/Sad"
song, but they didn't use it, they just sat
on it! The "Full Disclosure" scene was
also a highlight, especially Ami Stahlut's
cavorting Alice who got Lurch so excited
that he smiled and covered up his
excitement. Greg O'Leary's animations
of Fester flying to and becoming one
with the moon was something I hadn't
seen done before and it worked brilliantly.
Another highlight for me was Musical
Director Patrick Clancy's orchestration, it
was excellent particularly on some of the
underscore. I know this show quite well
but I heard things in the music I'd never
heard before, there was a spookiness
added to some of the songs, a discordant
ambience which worked very well.
The job of the director is to interpret the
source material for the medium you are
working in, and I believe that Mr O'Leary
did justice to the material here. He gave
us a funny, irreverent piece of theatre that
resonated with its audience and enabled
his performers to explore their roles and
worked with them to breathe life into their
characters. Or should that be death? The
choreography and music from the other
creatives added another marvellous layer
to a show that was a resounding success
for Oyster Lane.

Habit Forming
Based on the successful 1992 film
starring Whoppi Goldberg as a wise-
cracking lounge singer forced to go on the
lam after witnessing her boyfriend murder
a fellow hood, the musical was created
in 2006 with music by Alan Menken and
lyrics by Glenn Slater and was a hit around
the world. I saw it in the Civic Theatre in
Tallaght produced by Harold's Cross
Tallaght Musical Society on opening night,
Henchmen TJ (Jamie Place), Pablo (Paolo
Garau) and Joey (Alan Duffy) in Lady in the
Long Black Dress_
which was packed.
The show opened in a convent, 'Queen
of Angels' where a group of nuns were
attempting to sing, it was painful and
thankfully we moved quickly to the
Moonlight Lounge where Jenny McCabe
as Deloris, flanked by Abba'esque backing
singers, the 'Delorettes' were auditioning
to sing in the club, run by Deloris' boyfriend
Curtis, played with a subdued menace
by Eddie Brady. The songs, 'Take Me to
Heaven' and 'Fabulous, Baby!' were high-
octane disco numbers performed with a
wonderful panache and the 'Delorettes';
Leonna Condron, Kim Doran, Sarah
McGauran, Laura Medbury, Sally Sheerin
and Georgia Spooner produced some
great harmonies and subtle dance moves.
Told that she didn't get the gig, Deloris
decides to leave Curtis but witnesses him
murder one of his henchmen and runs to
her old school friend, policeman 'Sweaty'
Eddie, nicely played by Eoin Salley,
for help. Eddie places her in a witness
protection programme and brings her to
the 'Queen of Angels' convent. Here we
meet the Mother Superior, Julie Donnelly,
who sings the beautiful 'Here Within
These Walls'. Deloris sets out to win
the hearts and minds of the nuns she's
boarding with through a series of upbeat
numbers
infused
with
ecclesiastical
choral openings.  She teaches the nuns
how to sing and harmonise much to the
displeasure of the Mother Superior who
believes the devil may be at work through
the disco beats and soul singing.
Meanwhile, Deloris' boyfriend, Curtis
discovers where Deloris is holing up and
sets out to capture and 'dispose' of her.
Curtis' other henchmen, the hilarious TJ,
played by Jamie Place; the Latino 'lover'
Pablo, perfectly played by Paolo Garau
and self-styled "ladies' man" Joey, played
by Alan Duffy are like a cross between the
Bee Gees and the Three Stooges. They
infiltrate the convent but not before they
treat us to one of the shows' best numbers
'The Lady in The Long Black Dress' a
fabulous R&B tune redolent of 70's group
Tavares mixed with Barry White.
But it's the nuns who blessed this
show with pitch perfect singing and
superb
characterisations.
Delightful
performances from Charlene Masterson
as the hyper-active Sr Mary Patrick,
Rosaleen Nolan as the dour Sr Mary
Lazarus and Aoife Small as the demure Sr
Mary Robert - who's touching rendition of
'The Life I Never Led' was lovely and Mary
Galligan and Joan Kelly played Sr Mary
Theresa and Sr Mary Martin-of-Tours with
apostolic assurance.
Suffice to say, Deloris leads the nuns in
a series of wonderful numbers, appearing
on television and eventually singing for the
Pope. Curtis and his dastardly incompetent
flunkies get their comeuppance and Eddie
gets his girl.
The
musical
direction
by
Dermot
O'Callaghan was excellent, lovely work
with the harmonies on "Raise Your Voice"
and the other nun-led numbers and on
"Take Me to Heaven" and "Fabulous
Baby!" by Deloris and her backing singers.
The band were cloistered backstage, but
they sounded great with instrumentation
from Wah Guitar to splendid horns, it
was a musical trip through the '70s.
Choreography by Lea Carroll, clearly
working to her cast's strengths. It's not a
big dance show, there are just too many
nuns! But what she did do with them was
well-rehearsed and simple enough to look
good.
Wayne Handy created the set which was
all stained-glass window effects upstage
and on the side flats, with some other set
pieces trucked on an off to represent other
locations. Lighting by Tomás Fitzgerald
was very front of house heavy, more
side lighting would have added an extra
dimension to scenes. Sound by Vinny
Osborne was full range with each singer's
voice nicely reverbed, with pulsing bottom
end for the disco beats. Costumes by
Andrew Reddy were exceptional. The
range of colourful Nun's tabards was
fabulous. Deloris's club costume was of
the era and there was a lot of lame and
sequins throughout the show!
I attended the first performance and I
thought some of the scene changes were
a tad slow, I felt that the crew were not
well rehearsed. Miscuing in the lighting
department didn't help as some transitions
were in full lights.
Director Ciarán Mooney gave us a fairly
solid show, little artistic touches like the
Pope entering through the audience and
beefing up Deloris's backing singers and
adding a quirky slow-motion segment
during "Bless Our Show", elevated
it. However, it was Jenny McCabe's
performance as Deloris that raised the
show. She didn't try to emulate Whoppi
but made the character her own. Her wise-
cracking gangster's moll was straight out
of an MGM Musical and her comic timing
was delicious. Her naturalism midst a cast
of over-the-top caricatures was refreshing
and we were really rooting for her to
overcome her challenges. Ms. McCabe
also has a great voice with a superbly
broad range. She shone in the big disco
numbers and brought it down with skill on
the title song, which is one of the better
songs in the show. Ms. McCabe was
Deloris Van Cartier, not just a sister act but
a class act.

Hello Dolly!
Coolmine Musical Society (CMS) has
been around since 1981 and has won
many AIMS awards since then and played
to many thousands of Dublin theatregoers
with their innovative takes on modern and
classical musicals. Their latest offering
was Dolly Parton's "9 to 5" which took
to the Draíocht stage in November of
this year. Directed by Pat McElwain with
Nicole McDonald on dance duty and Dave
McGauran looking after the music, I was
curious as to what these three award-
winning creatives would do with the
material.
Written in 2009 and based on a film made
and set in the late '70's early '80's about
office politics and a misogynist boss
vs his rebelling staff. It is an engagingly
old fashioned, simple story full of Dolly
songs and lewd slapstick, with a cartoon
thin plot and corny comedy; but with
great roles for female performers, which
is a nice change.  The plot follows the
chaotic adventures of three downtrodden
women struggling under the chauvinistic
oppression of the good ole boy network
of business and office politics. The three
musketeers take their revenge not only
on their sexist, misogynist boss, but also
on global sexism and prejudice infecting
office culture of the '80s.
John O'Donoghue's set was full of clean
lines, sharp colours and was built by Jim
Whelan and painted by Ben Hennessy, it
looked great. Incorporating a video screen
upstage, which showed the Dolly welcome
video, plus the occasional image and a
ticking clock. The side flats and headers
and the gobos on the floor all worked
together to create a corporate image
where time was of the essence. The desks
on castors were smooth and fabulously
mobile and Hart's office, complete with
his portrait was perfect. It was into this
no-nonsense corporate environment we
met our three heroines: Violet, a struggling
widow played by Bronwyn Andrews;
Doralee, the boss's PA played by Serena
Salmon; and newcomer to the firm, the
nervous Judy played by Nicole Lamb.
Ms Andrews as Violet had poise and grace
and a wonderfully expressive voice; Nicole
Lamb's Judy was all nervous twitches and
low self-worth, her character's journey
to independence was marvellously done
and her voice on "Get Out and Stay
Out" brought the house down. But it was
Serena Salmon's Doralee who stole the
show for me. The more difficult role of the
three in that it is clearly modelled on Dolly,
and often played as an impersonation
rather that a character. Ms Salmon did not
fall into that trap and gave us a superbly
nuanced performance of a Doralee who
was 'mad as hell and not going to take
it anymore'. Her scene with Hart where
she attacks him was pure drama and
her singing on "Backwoods Barbie" was
tender, wistful, and powerful.
As
the
"sexist,
egotistical,
lying,
hypocritical bigot", Kevin Hartnett played
Franklin Hart (the nameplate on his desk
read: F Hart) with outrageous misogyny.
His performance of "Here for You" was
so sleazy it went beyond humour and
ventured into Weinstein territory, which
was very difficult to watch but served to
justify the three ladies' extreme retaliation.
Mr Hartnett's performance was excellent.
Hart totally ignored the person who was
really in love with him (except to bully her
into doing his dirty work), office manager
Roz Keith. Played here with unfettered
glee by Jenny Seery. Ms Seery was by far
the funniest character on stage, yet she
also got across the sad pathos of Roz.
Her performance of "Heart to Hart" was
hilarious and on "5 to 9" quite mournful.
The love interests of our three amigos were
very different to each other; Joe the office
junior accountant was sweet on Violet,
played by Daire Kelly in Clark Kent mode
with the glasses and stoic demeanour and
a fine singing voice; Doralee's husband,
Dwayne played with Texan assurance by
Ciarán Lenehan and Judy's ex-husband
Dick played with a distasteful oiliness
by Liam Egan. Whilst the three male
characters are pure stereotypes, all three
actors played them with a total sincerity,
which was refreshing. Violet's other male
in her life was her teenage son, Josh,
played here by Eoin Kenny in a nicely
tuned performance.
The office had its share of quirky
characters such as Maureen, the office
drunk. Liberally sipping from her hip flask,
Maureen was played by Kathryn Gibbons
with a nice restraint. Michelle Harris played
Maria Delgado, who is curious about
the running of the company and gets
fired and rehired. Ms Harris spoke some
of her lines in Spanish, which was very
effective. Valerie Andrews played Kathy,
one of the more no-nonsense characters
with assurance. When Russell Tinsworthy
the CEO of the Company, played with an
avuncular calmness by Justin Parkes,
visits he promotes and demotes with a
modern political correctness I feel was
absent back in the early '80s. But it served
as a happy ever after.
Director Pat McElwain's attention to detail
was so meticulous it permeated the
entire production: from Dave McGauran's
wonderful arrangement of both orchestra
and chorus to Nicole McDonald's clever,
innovative at times, choreography; Gerry
McCann's excellent stage management
team; Denis Twomey's pin-sharp lighting;
Jody Trehy's well-balanced sound and
Ali Murphy's excellent make-up and
wigs. But he's right to be so meticulous
and I wish more directors were as
conscientious about their craft as Mr
McElwain is. The attention to detail on this
show was wonderful. From the clean lines
of the set to the accuracy of the props and
the smoothness of the transitions to the
commitment of the performers - the show
jumped off the stage bright and cheery
like a newly minted penny.
The production had some nice ideas too,
such as: the flying sequence where Hart
was suspended at the end of Act I (most
societies don't do this because of cost or
resources); the multiple Roz characters; a
projection of Violet on the cover of 'Time'
magazine and so on. The production
values were high on this show, from
costuming to set painting and lighting
- the show looked brilliant, all colour-
matched and blended and very classy.
Mr McElwain did push the more ribald
elements of the story to the fore at times
e.g. Hart's footballs, Roz's antics on the
floor in front of him and on the sofa, but it
was all done in the "worst" possible taste,
which the audience absolutely loved!

show_raw: Joseph And The Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat
review_text:
What's not to love about Joseph? It
has great music, an array of character
roles, plenty of opportunities for dance
and interpretation, a good smattering
of comedy… and it's short! On a
wintry night, with a long drive ahead
of me after the show, it was great to
be on the road at 10.15pm, thoroughly
entertained, humming the familiar songs
and remembering the key moments of a
delightfully uplifting production.
This was a very tidy, by-the-book
production by Director, Kevin Kennedy,
enhanced
by
some
lovely
comedy
touches, and nicely directed principal
action. The simple but effective set meant
few delays throughout, and the selection
of props and furniture added greatly to the
fun. The pace throughout was very good,
and the principals had well-established
character. There was good attention to
atmospheric lighting, and sound quality
allowed for every line to be clearly heard.
Perhaps the Narrator could have had
a change of costume for the second
act but costuming throughout was very
good. My only niggle was that on a few
occasions, when Joseph and the narrator
were dancing with the chorus, they were
the only ones not singing, and while the
Narrator was strong and secure, I did feel
she needed a confidence boost to be
more exaggerated in some of her comedy.
These are, however, minor criticisms
of an otherwise very strong and secure
production.
Choreographer, James Dobbs, kept the
pace and action on stage varied, creative
and well-disciplined. The wives and
brothers performed their routines with
panache, and the bigger chorus numbers
were alive with energy and enthusiasm.
There were nice comedic touches too,
with a fun routine during Those Canaan
Days, and maybe a slightly less successful
dance for Mrs. Potiphar, but the overall
choreographic contribution to the show
was extremely positive.
Definitely a highlight of the show was the
quality of the music, both from the pit,
