Another superb performance was Eoin
Sheedy as Mr Mushnik. I loved his
character; pure NYC complete with
accent and Jewish mannerisms. He sang
well on "Ya Never Know" and with great
funny subtext on "Mushnik and Son". His
Mushnik was quite caring, despite him
being a bit of a monster towards Seymour,
and the audience loved him. Audrey's
egotistical misogynist boyfriend, Oran,
was played by Ciarán Collins. He was
uber-misogynist, snarky, full of himself
and I suspect gave Audrey II indigestion!
Oran can be overplayed, like a panto or
cartoon-baddie, but Mr Collins played
him with a smoothness rather than an
over-the-top caricature. "Dentist" was
a highlight of the production as was his
various cameos later in the show!
Many shows are written with a Greek
Chorus, it's a great narrative device that
goes back to the dawn of theatre. Think
of 'Legally Blonde' or 'Joseph and the
Technicolor Dreamcoat' or 'Urinetown',
their function is to provide exposition
or commentary on the action. For the
Greek Chorus or 'Ronnettes' as they are
sometimes called in this show, we had
Clíodhna McNelis as Crystal, Lauren
Dunne as Ronnette, Kate Barrett as Chiffon
and Lauren-Kate Browne as Diamond.
The addition of the Diamond character
allowed for a more rounded sound from
the group, and it just looked better. All four
performers were individually very good but
when together became excellent. They
were perfectly cast; they didn't look alike
at all, but they gelled perfectly onstage.
They hung around the set like they owned
it and had an easy nonchalance at times,
observing and commenting through song
and interacting as local characters with
the principals and were an integral part of
the success of this production as were the
'wranglers' of Audrey II.
Puppeteer, Dara O'Callaghan did some
lovely work in what is usually, quite an
unwieldly puppet plant(s)! The unsung hero
of the show as without him, the audience
wouldn't believe. He made Audrey II lip
sync quite well with the songs and come
alive when 'she' was feeding! Audrey II
was voiced by Colm McGuinness. Mr
McGuinness has the most incredibly
expressive voice; I cannot imagine many
being able to do what he does. His
phrasing, resonance and texture were
sublime in this show. When a performer
voices a puppet and is not seen by the
audience like here and on 'Avenue Q' for
example, their voice must do all the work
of creating the character. Mr McGuinness'
voice effortlessly portrayed Audrey II's
character and the audience were wowed
by it. From "Feed Me (Git it)" up to the
final song (where we did see him) "Mean
Green Mother" Mr McGuinness gave us a
remarkable interpretation of Audrey II.
Excellent stage management from Ted
Germaine and his crew, rotating the
revolve on cue was quite a feat and it
worked perfectly. A fully rounded sound
from Star Systems and great lighting
from Indigo Lighting added to the high
production values on show. Super set
design, construction and dressing with
Karen Barrett's range of 1960's costumes
and plant specials coupled with good hair
and make-up all added up to an excellent
production which the audience and I,
absolutely loved. Well done!

Elvis has left the Building!
Joe DiPietro's homage to Americana
and the birth of the teenager was given
the Galway University Musical Society
treatment in late January, early February
this year. Written for the stage in 2004, this
jukebox musical featuring songs made
famous by Elvis Presley, is very popular
around the world. Whilst the characters
and plot twists conjure the sparring lovers
and surprise couplings of Shakespeare's
'Much Ado About Nothing', 'Twelfth
Night', 'As You Like It' and 'A Midsummer
Night's Dream', the musical is a window
on a time when children became adults
without the awkwardness and rebellion of
the teenage years. The idea of mashing up
the Bard's plot devices with Elvis' songs is
certainly an audacious one, but somehow
it works. Of course, the super-objective
of the whole enterprise is heralding of the
birth of the 'teenager'', and 'borrowing'
from 'Footloose' the harbinger is an
enigmatic stranger.
So, to the plot: Chad, played here by
Robert Cosgrove, arrives in a small dusty
town on his faulty motorbike looking for
a mechanic, having just been released
from prison. He meets Natalie, played
by Hannah Cogan, the local tomboy
mechanic and she falls for his roguish
charms. Chad however falls for Miss
Sandra, played by Laura Toolis, the
bookish curator of the local museum.
Natalie dresses as a guy to get her guy,
believing that he'll fall for her if she is
more like him, and the other townsfolk
all fall for each other. There are a couple
of sub-plots in the show, which were not
fully realised in Tara Mackin's direction,
but it's a simple plot, a parody, which is
oven-ready for a director to get their teeth
into to make it their own. However, I don't
think Ms Mackin focussed enough on the
parodic aspects of the work.
Playing Chad, Robert Cosgrove certainly
had all the moves and a cracking voice
to boot. When he arrived in the sleepy
little town, he took control of the younger
citizens through the force of is personality
and by questioning authority. When
Mr Cosgrove sang "I Don't Want To",
it was heartfelt and poignant with self-
depreciation and confusion. However, he
spoke directly with the audience during
this song rather than it being an internal
monologue, which lessened its impact.
His other numbers were also good, but
the above song really showed off his very
pleasant tone and range. His duets with
Natalie/Ed and Jim were also super and he
displayed a powerful voice when needed.
His acting as Chad was somewhat let
down by his costume, the leather jacket
seemed about two sizes too big for him,
was not tight fitting nor a biker's jacket,
so he didn't strut around the stage as the
alpha male he was meant to be. He got
better when he dropped it and just wore
the t-shirt.
Natalie/Ed was played winningly by
Hannah Cogan. She really nailed Natalie's
character early on. Her unwashed hair
and dirty overalls added to the tomboy
look. Her transformation to Ed was less
successful and again inattention to detail
was to blame here. When she put the 'oil'
on her face and donned Chad's jacket and
wore Dennis' hat, she didn't really alter her
physicality. Her hair was still visible, and
the jeans were far too wide-legged and
modern. That said her singing on "Blue
Suede Shoes" as Ed was great as was
her "Follow That Dream" both with Chad.
Cian Elwood played Dennis, the nerdish
roustabout wannabe who was in love with
Natalie. He had a range of twitches, brays,
and dithering which he presented to
great effect. He used his head voice very
efficiently too, giving Dennis a childish
bearing. A very good performance full
of longing for Natalie and a desire to be
like Chad. His comic timing was also
excellent, as was his energy and he sang
well throughout.
As Natalie's father, Jim, James Boylan
could have been aged up a bit more, he
seemed far too young to play Natalie's
father. He did have a lovely chemistry
with Sylvia however and their scenes did
convince. Sylvia was beautifully played
by Teniola Olaleye, who is blessed with a
fabulous voice, her rendition of "There's
Always Me" was full of emotion and
longing and stole the show.
On arrival in town, Chad falls for the town
museum curator, Miss Sandra played by
Laura Toolis. Ms Toolis was a fabulous
Sandra. She personified the intellectual
academic, revelling in Shakespeare and
culture. Her scene in the museum with
'Ed', when she fell for 'him' was very
well played as was her contemptuous
dismissal of Chad. Her singing on "Let
Yourself Go" was super and she was great
in "Teddy Bear/Hound Dog" with Chad,
Dennis & Natalie.
The sub-plot of a romance blossoming
between Sylvia's daughter, Lorraine and
the Mayor's son Dean was sweetly done.
Lorraine was played by Eimear Wolohan
and she was perfectly cast, playing the 16
year old as young and a bit vague. Looking
like a young Mia Goth, Ms Wolohan owned
her character and was a good foil for Cian
Hughes as Dean. There was a lovely gentle
quality to Mr Hughes' performance. He
had a wholesome chemistry with Lorraine
and "It's Now or Never" was quite nice, if a
little off-key. Dean's mother, Mayor Matilda
Hyde was played by Abby Doran in a
scenery chewing performance that was all
pantomime baddie. Clearly unhinged and
in danger of loosing 'her' town, Ms Doran
turned her incredulousness up to eleven
as she demanded everybody be shot. Her
sidekick, the silent Sheriff Earl was played
with an undercurrent of frustration by Leo
Andal. The ensemble in this production
was full of energy and youthful enthusiasm
and nailed the big complicated choral
numbers with confidence. Musical director
Killian Cogan gave us some beautiful
arrangements of "Heartbreak Hotel" and
"Can't Help Falling in Love" and his band
were quite tight, especially the electric
guitar which was the backbone of the
production. Dance duties were looked
after by choreographer Aoibh Tully. Ms
Tully devised some intricate and pleasing
routines, at times the ensemble was not
quite in sync, so some of the routines
looked untidy.
Lighting by Mick Byrne and sound by
Fintan Higgins were good if not remarkable
and stage management by Kate O'Dowd
was solid. There was no set as such
just some set pieces brought on and off
to set scene locations. The bar, tables
and chairs worked in Sylvia's and the
'tunnel of love' upstage in Act 2, looked
suitably garish. However, the Garage
scenes could have been better dressed
and Chad's Honda 50 motorcycle didn't
work! Some of the costumes were of the
era and very colourful. The angels and
devil's costumes looked okay. The gowns
and men's suits at the end added to the
atmosphere of love being strengthened
after all the chaos. However, Chad's and
'Ed's' costumes were too modern, but the
band's striped tops looked great!
'All Shook Up' is written as a farcical
comedy of errors, mistaken identity,
and subterfuge. It holds a mirror up to
small town America of the fifties and its
evangelical draconian rules and celebrates
the birth of the 'teenager' through Chad's
rebellion against authority.  But first and
foremost, it's a comedy that should be
played tongue in cheek. GUMS production
didn't feel like a parody or a farce, it was
too loose and most of the 'jokes' fell flat.
The pace was good though and it did rattle
and roll along quite fast, as it should. More
attention to detail on costumes would
have made a huge difference, especially
Chad's jacket, it was a glaring error and
diminished Chad's character which made
his character less effective on stage.
Chad represents the 'new' America and
as he says he travels around spreading
his 'love', but this is an allegory of Chad
as a prophet disseminating the news
that the old ways no longer cut it. He is
a rebel with a definite cause and should
be charismatic, charming, larger than life
and very different to the young people he
encounters.

A few years ago, Mel Brooks and Thomas
Meehan decided to write a musical
based on Brooks' 1974 film about Mary
Shelley's Frankenstein. This was kind of in
response to the success he had with 'The
Producers'. 'Young Frankenstein' was a
big hit for Brooks and his co-writer Gene
Wilder who also starred in the title role.
The making of the film is now the stuff
of legend as much of it was improvised
and workshopped, showing a cast and
director at the height of their powers. The
musical uses a lot of the same script plus
some of the songs are sort of based on
the original actors' interpretations of their
characters. So, it's not an easy show to
produce because it will rise or fall based
on the success of the casting.
And so, it came to be that I was in Solstice
Arts Centre on 17 February this year to
see Trim Musical Theatre Society's version
of the musical praying that it would be
good as it's one of my favorite films. It's
an eminently quotable iconic film, like
'Withnail & I', 'The Princess Bride' or 'The
Rocky Horror Picture Show' and many
other similar relatively low-budget movies,
so it was important that they got it right!
Well, dear reader I should tell you straight
away that they did. It
was marvelous, funny, fast and accurate
with a stunning cast, a creepy set, great
band and crazy choreography - all drawn
together by director Pat McElwain and his
creatives.
Musical director Dermot O'Callaghan
conducted an eleven-piece band that
appeared to enjoy the show as much as
we did! Their playing was light and bouncy,
hitting the different styles just right. Jazzy,
bluesy with a hint of Vaudeville plus the
underscore straight out of a 1930's horror
film - all was interpreted to perfection.
Laura Douglas choreography was full of
energy and madcap fun, with the "Puttin'
on the Ritz" shadow dancing sequence
being a standout. There's not a lot of big
dance numbers in the show but I loved
"Don't Touch Me" with the passengers
and "Welcome to Transylvania" was
well blocked and moved and very funny.
John O'Donoghue's set design looked
fabulous, it was not a replica of the film set
but had its own quirkiness. The lights and
huge switches on the lab machines, the
fireworks upstage on the bed all added to
that old school 1930's feel. The revolving
bookshelf was great and allowed for
some slapstick fun. But the best bit was
the carriage with the actors' playing
horses, that really worked. Constructed
and dressed by Ben Hennessey and Jim
Whelan, the set was not meant to be
perfect, more like a movie set on an Ed
Wood film; quirky, wobbly and a bit cheap
looking. In other words, ideal!
The performers acted their socks off in this
show and seemed to be having great fun
doing it, which transferred to the audience
who loved every minute. Each cast
member clearly understood the genre, the
humour and how to play it. The physical
comedy was great, the double takes, the
madcap moments of pure mayhem all
worked. Some scenes seemed to have
been workshopped and played with as
they gave off a lovely immediacy and
freshness. The actors seemed to enjoy the
script, the faux German accents, rolling it
around their mouths before expelling it in
moments of great comic timing.
So, for those of you unlucky to have
missed the film and especially Trim's
musical take on it, here's the plot: In
Transylvania,
Dr
Victor
Frankenstein
(maker of monsters) has just died, and his
estate is left to his grandson Frederick, a
surgeon in New York. He travels there to
sell the castle and meets Inga, Igor and
a host of other characters who convince
him to carry on his grandfather's work. He
creates his own monster and raises the ire
of the local villagers who want to burn him
out. It's a silly plot and clearly parodies
the James Whale 1931 film, but it's the
characters that make it funny rather than
the situation, although that becomes
hilarious once they veer away from the
original.
Leading the cast was Colin Flynn as
Frederick Frankenstein (or Fronkenstein
as he insisted on being called early in
the show). Mr Flynn had great comic
timing and a frenetic physicality that was
so energetic it was tiring to watch! His
singing was good on "Together Again"
with Igor and "Man About Town" &
"Puttin' on the Ritz". But it was his clear
love for the character that came over to
us the audience. He seemed to embrace
the madness of Frederick and played it
to the hilt without hamming it up, difficult
in a show that is all ham! Playing his
servant, Igor, was Damien Douglas. His
mannerisms, his timing, his accent was
all perfect in an idiosyncratic performance
where he made the character his own.
Frederick's lab assistant, Inga, was played
by Louise Cassidy. She was super in the
role, just the right amount of innocence
and seduction. Frederick's fiancé, who he
leaves behind in New York, was played by
Jenny McCabe who's timing and singing
were flawless. I loved "Please Don't Touch
Me", where the timing is everything and
she nailed it. She transformed into the
Bride of Frankenstein quite well too, with
the Elsa Lanchester hairdo and unbridled
sensuality.
As the monster we had Chris Corroon.
He was so tall in the massive platform
boots yet managed to run and dance
with much energy risking an ankle injury
at least! His timing was also excellent,
and his range of monosyllabic grunts
was quite impressive. His scene with the
Kevin Hartnett's Hermit was a highlight
of the show. Mr Hartnett's Hermit was so
sad, much more so than the film and his
singing on "Please Send Me Someone"
was excellent. Playing the Housekeeper,
Frau Blücher, we had Siobhan Fawsitt.
Her timing on the Ovaltine
scene with Frederick was flawless as was
her singing on "He Vas My Boyfriend".
Whenever her name was mentioned
in the show, a sound effect of horses
neighing was heard. We also had Sean
Fox as the local Police Inspector, Hans
Kemp, who had lost an arm and a leg to
the original (Victor's) monster. The limp
was great, as was the arm business.
His accent was good too and he never
dropped it. Mr Fox's comic timing was
good, and he sang well on "Law" with the
villagers. He was often accompanied by
the Village Idiot, Ziggy who was played
by Eoin Kenny. Mr Kenny adopted a
hilarious gormless expression and his
antics with the gun, where he always
pointed it backwards, were great. Again,
great comic timing and super delivery.
Finally, we had a surprise appearance
by Frederick's Grandfather, Victor, in a
dream-like sequence. Played by Ronan
Walsh, he gave us a super character, quite
the dad figure with Frederick encouraging
him to continue his work. There was an
ensemble cast too, playing villagers and
New York citizens and others, who sang
and danced throughout with great energy.
This cast were marvellous. United in their
appreciation for the show, they worked
together to get the humour across, and it
did. The audience loved it. It looked like
a B-movie, with Ali Murphy's fabulous
make-up and wigs, Miriam Donnelly's
great costumes, Darren Kelleher's spooky
lighting and Alan White's full band sound
and great sound effects all held together
by stage manager Frank Connolly.
Pat McElwain directed this show with
a light and delicate touch, allowing the
comedy to flow without forcing it. His
interpretation was excellent, and it rattled
along like a horse and carriage on the way
up to the Castle. I loved his little touches
like the horses and the werewolf and the
Jenga and fireworks on the table. The
production looked good, with minimum
fuss in the transitions keeping it fast
paced yet he allowed it to breathe at
times. Excellent work.

Les Mis meets Phantom
Produced by Tipperary Musical Society
with choreography by Stephanie Browne,
musical direction by Mary Rose McNally
and direction by Paul Norton; 'The
Hunchback of Notre Dame' was staged in
the Simon Ryan Theatre in Tipperary from
13th to 18th February. It is an odd musical,
it's like a cross between 'Les Miserables'
and 'The Phantom of the Opera' scored
by Disney regulars Alan Menken and
Stephen Schwartz. Originally written as a
novel by Victor Hugo in 1831, the stage
production of the 1996 animated Disney
film has been around since it was first
produced in Germany in 1999. Although
there have been changes from the film,
some of that American 'Disneyness'
remains in some of the characters and in
some of the text. That said, large swathes
of Hugo's novel remain, and these are to
my ears the more successful servings of
the show.
The story explores love, lust and faith
in 15th century Paris and focuses on
Quasimodo, a deformed bellringer, his
uncle the Archdeacon Frollo and a Romani
girl called Esmerelda with whom they both
fall in love and is set in and around the
Notre Dame cathedral. The opening of
the show blew everyone away; the set,
lighting and most of all the choral singing
on "Olim" was fabulous.
Musical director, Mary Rose McNally
conducted a sixteen-piece orchestra
to bring us the big, sumptuous sound
demanded of the score. Her interpretation
was excellent, and I particularly liked
the strings which were lush and full. The
ever-present choir sited upstage on the
platform and below nailed the complex
harmonies and were powerful. Most of
the leads were very well cast and the
'Gypsy' numbers were particularly vibrant
mostly due to choreographer Stephanie
Browne's work. It was full of energy,
especially on "Tavern Song", "Rhythm
of the Tambourine" and "The Court of
Miracles". The crowd scenes were nicely
blocked and looked natural, and the
ensemble were meticulously rehearsed.
Most of the actors in this show really
engaged with the style set by the
creatives and there were some stand-
out performances on the night I saw it.
Emmet Donlon played the title role and
had a great physicality as Quasimodo.
He dropped his head and trunk down
and rounded his back to create the effect
of his kyphosis. This was particularly
effective and lowered his status among
the other performers. His singing was
also very good, especially on "Heaven's
Light" and "Out There". He had a great
chemistry with Frollo and his portrayal of
the character's attraction to Esmerelda
was subtle and heart-breaking. As Frollo,
Derek Ryan was quite mesmerising to
watch, his wonderful voice brought out
all the character's emotion particularly
on "Hellfire". His acting portrayed Frollo's
devotion to God, his reluctant care
for Quasimodo and his inner conflict
with his desire for Esmerelda and his
hatred for the Gypsies. As Esmerelda,
Madeline Blackwell stole every scene
she was in and did it effortlessly and, I
suspect, unconsciously. Her portrayal
of Esmerelda was complete; her singing
was sublime, and she had a beautiful tone
and a wonderful presence. Her dance
was excellent and full of character and
her acting, particularly the scenes with
Frollo, was heartfelt and luminous. Ms
Blackwell is a performer to watch. These
three performers were ably supported by
a great ensemble, who played multiple
roles including gargoyles! These gargoyle
characters should not have worked - they
are quite contemporary in their text, like
a leftover form the animated film and
seem out of balance with the style of the
production. However, their stillness and
vocals and empathy with Quasimodo was
excellent and it is a testament to their
skills that they integrated flawlessly into
the story.
Another potential suitor for Esmerelda
was Captain Phoebus de Martin as played
by Adam Skeffington. He played him more
like a Disney Prince rather than a Hugo
character, which seemed to be at odds
with the rest of the cast and the director's
intention. However, once the character
was injured and less the Alpha Male, his
acting improved immensely, and we could
see why Esmerelda was attracted to him.
His singing on "Someday" with Esmerelda
was lovely. Another character worthy of
mention was that of James O'Donovan's
Clopin, the King of the Gypsies. He strode
around the stage with high status and
like a ring master orchestrated much
of the action. Mr O'Donovan's accent
and
mannerisms
whilst
playful
and
grandstanding, belied the darker nature
of the character, which he revealed at
poignant points during the show. His
singing was excellent on "Topsy Turvey"
and during The Court of Miracles scene.
He also had a magician quality where he
would disappear in a puff of smoke!
Other performances to included Cormac
Maher as Jehan, Frollo's brother and
father to Quasimodo, who played his
death scene very well; Kevin Reade as St
Aphrodisius who had the skills and gravitas
of making a headless character work and
he sang with passion; Lorraine Cormack
as Florika, Quasimodo's mother a feisty,
free-spirited character; Conor Ryan as
Father Dupin, a lovely performance as the
guardian of Frollo and Jehan. Jason Ryan
as Frederick, Cole Flanagan as King Louis,
Lena Hally as Madame, Tadgh O'Connor
as Gypsy Singer and Dave Condon as
Gentleman all played with energy, passion
and were totally on point.
Aidan O'Connell's set design was super.
The platforms were at a good height and
the chess board-like floor added a nice
detail. The moving platform was used with
restraint, and I liked how the performers
could climb up the upstage corner
uprights. The festoon bunting and clothing
really changed the space for the outdoor
scenes and the bell rope looked great as
did the brought on wooden rails to create
the top of the church. The platform for
the Fool and burning scenes worked well
too. Lovely attention to detail and clever
use and re-use of materials created a set
with depth and purpose. Stage manager
Alma Quinn marshalled everything with
an enviable tightness. Transitions and
scene changes were quick and faultless.
Excellent work. Costume and make-up
were flawless and with excellent lighting
by Alan McCormack and lovely sound by
Star Systems, it really was a feast for the
ears and eyes.
Paul Norton directed with a lot of sensitivity
and managed to wrestle the work into
a moving spectacle. It's not a perfect
stage musical in that there are still some
hangovers from the Disney animated film,
which do not work on stage, but the music
is great, and Mr Norton elicited some
superb performances from the cast. The
whole production looked very high quality
from the set to the costumes, we felt like
we were in Paris in 1482. Mr Norton paced
the show very well and we felt empathy
with some of the characters. The addition
of sign- language towards the end of the
show was a nice touch as Quasimodo
was deaf from the bells and there was a
palpable energy during the more rousing
scenes. The transformations of actor to
Quasimodo and back again at the start
and end of the show was an interesting
device that highlighted one of the themes
of the piece, that of inner beauty trumping
outer attractiveness. It was very enjoyable
by all, the audience gave the company a
well-deserved lengthy standing ovation.

En Passant
Tim Rice and the two lads from Abba
(Björn Ulvaeus and Benny Andersson)
wrote 'Chess' in 1984 and it's one of
those marmite musicals that you either
love or loath. It has some great tunes and
a good story but when you listen to the
original recording it sounds awfully dated.
It was first released as a concept album,
like 'Evita' and 'Jesus Christ Superstar' -
two of Rice's earlier collaborations with
Andrew Lloyd-Webber, and was eventually
made into a stage show in 1986. Maybe
it's the synth infused score mixed with the
OTT orchestrations that date it, but it's not
an easy listen. So, it's a real challenge for
a production company to make it work in
2023.
Athlone Musical Society took up the
challenge and staged it in the Dean Crowe
Theatre in March of this year. Directed
by Alfie Kilduff with musical direction by
Ger Madden and choreography by Jay
Molyneux, this was a sumptuous looking
production, colour coordinated in black
and white with dashes of reds and blues
and an MTV staging, good sound, and
brilliant vocals from committed singers,
especially the onstage choir and a cast of
well-known musical theatre performers.
The story takes place at the World Chess
Championships in Merano, Italy and
Bangkok, Thailand one year apart at the
height of the Cold War between the Soviet
Union and the USA. The Russian, Anatoly,
and the American, Freddie, compete, not
just at chess, but for the affections of
Freddie's assistant and second, Florence.
Conspiratorial mind games by Anatoly's
compatriot Molokov, and the journalist/
CIA informant Walter, play out as Anatoly's
wife Svetlana arrives adding to the
difficulties. The Arbiter, basically a referee,
acts as a narrator, so that we don't get too
lost in the politics of the post-World War II
superpowers.
It was an open staging, so we could see
the set when we sat down at the start,
with a video screen and benches for the
choir, it was quite modern looking. I liked
the big chess pieces framing the space
and the chess board patterns on the floor
and on some of the props e.g. the drinks
trays. The brick effect flats looked good
and added depth and texture to the stage
and the black upstage doors were a great
addition, particularly as the performers
had to climb treads to the chessboard.
Kudos to scenic artist Anna Boles too,
whose paint work was admirable. It was
lit by Ronan Kenny who went all out with
"One Night in Bangkok", using every light
in the rig to great effect yet brought it
down beautifully though the use of sharp
specials. The sound by Derek Recks was
also superb, lovely balance between band
and singers and he managed to get a full,
rich sound across to the audience with
subtle reverb on the mics.
Musical director and conductor Ger
Madden made what is frankly a tired score
sound new and fresh. The music is rooted
in overblown orchestrations and '80's
synths complete with syn drums and the
odd electric guitar lick as a throwback to
the 70's, but Mr Madden wisely eschewed
the Abba sound and gave us a very
contemporary sounding score. His band
of ten players at times sounded like a full
orchestra, such was his and their skill.
Flute and horns were great as was the
guitar, particularly in Freddie's songs. The
rhythm section of percussion and bass
drove the whole show with a relentless
beat, and I loved the odd bit of xylophone.
The choir were superb, their harmonies
on "Merano", "Hymn to Chess" and
"Anthem" were beautiful and as we could
always see them, we connected with them
throughout. Having the choir visible and
invested in the action of the piece was one
of the high points of the show. Not only
was their singing most excellent but they
doubled as ensemble at times; cheering
on Freddie; waving flags for Anatoly and
generally providing crown noise for the
bigger scenes. They also looked great
and sported several hand-held props and
simple costumes. They were arranged
in their black or white shirts diagonally
across the benches upstage and looked
and sounded fantastic.
Choreography was handled by the
ubiquitous Jay Molyneux who gave us
a great selection of styles on this show.
There was much to like in the show, I
loved the white gloves and the 'Durga'
routine, which was repeated. I also liked
some of the choreography during the
chess games and "Golden Bangkok / One
Night in Bangkok" was very well moved
and a great second act opener with lots of
energy and sexual tension.
Director Alfie Kilduff seemed to focus most
of his energies on the presentation of the
songs and at times it was like watching
a 'Concert' version of 'Chess'. Florence
and Molotov were the notable exceptions
here. A lot of the cool looking visuals were
kept for the song performances too, so
that when the actor was singing it looked
like they were in a concert or an MTV
video. Almost every song was performed
downstage and out to the audience and
not in the location where it was meant to
be set or to another performer.
Playing Freddie was Derek Collins who
looked great in his white suit and
relaxed attitude, he was every inch
the brash American. He had a good
relationship with Florence during the
newspaper scene and his scene with
Anatoly in Act II, when he is trying to help
him was good. His singing was good and
"One Night in Bangkok" was powerful,
with loads of energy and a great vocal. As
Florence we were fortunate to have Lucia
Evans. She was absolutely the star of
this production. Her vocal was incredibly
poignant at times, full of
expression, angst and feeling and at
others just showstopping in its range. Her
duet with Svetlana "I Know him so Well",
was excellent and they bounced well off
each other, and she brought the house
down with her solos. Her acting was
also good, she was invested in her fellow
performers and had a great chemistry with
Molotov in particular. Ms Evans owned the
role gave us the most three- dimensional
and rounded character in the show. As
the third wheel in the love triangle, we had
Anatoly, the Russian, played by Shane
Kelly in a soft brooding performance. He
sang well throughout but especially on
"Anthem", where he was backed by the
fabulous choir and gave a fitting lift to the
end of Act I.
Emily Lohan played Svetlana, Anatoly's
abandoned wife. Ms Lohan can turn her
hand to any role and here she perfected
the accent and showed the character's
pain and anguish and sang well on "I
Know him so Well" with Florence and on
"Someone Else's Story" which is not often
performed in productions of the show, but
Athlone got permission. Kori Kilduff played
the Arbiter with fierce focus and control.
She held the stage with her presence
and had a passivity in her performance
that was quite riveting to watch. She
sang very well throughout, and exuded
confidence. As Walter, a TV presenter for
Global News but also possibly in league
with the CIA, Kieran Kilduff gave off a
quiet confidence and was often seen on
stage just observing. He played his sub-
text quite subtly and sang quite well on
the few songs he was in. Joe Steiner
was brilliant as Molokov. He had great
accent both in song and in dialogue and a
wonderful energy as the devious Russian.
He eclipsed others in every scene such
was his focus, except Florence where he
had a wonderful dynamic and they were
equal. His singing was great especially
on "The Soviet Machine". Paul Holloway
played The Mayor. Mr Holloway had a
fine presence on stage and sang well on
"Merano". I also believe that I spotted him
in other roles during the show...
The ensemble was very adaptable,
becoming
many
different
characters
from Russian Embassy Staff to dancers
to guests, they were aided and abetted
by the ever-present choir and populated
certain scenes with energy and presence.
Cherise O'Moore's costumes looked very
natural. Great range of costumes for
the dancers especially the Thai look in
"Golden Bangkok' and the black and
white clad dancers and a great range
of masks. The suits looked super, and I
loved Molotov's red leather coat. Make-
up was unaccredited but looked good.
Hair by Rosaleen West was perfect, with
Freddie looking dishevelled and Anatoly
looking pristine. Stage manager Jonathan
O'Brien and his crew were very stealthy,
we hardly saw them. The transitions were
quick and accurate, and he organised and
assembled his cast and ensemble very
well.
There was a lot to admire here, it just
didn't gel as a musical theatre production.
So, yes Athlone certainly did rise to the
challenge and were successful in bringing
'Chess' to the audience, just not in the
form expected.

After
a
significant
break
from
performance, Covid-enforced, Director
Donal Henderson was coerced into
action by the desire of so many to get
them back on stage, and in selecting
Peter Pan - A Musical Adventure, he
found a piece that catered for the older
established members and offered the very
enthusiastic youth side of the company
something to get their teeth into. As
a whole community experience, this
was a good choice indeed. Two things,
however, both beyond his control, stood
in the way of him achieving the level of
fantasy and creativity that he might have
desired. Firstly, the performance venue
was very restrictive, with a small stage,
little wing space or storage space, and
limited technical facilities. Secondly, the
quality of the backing tracks, supplied by
the licensor, was extremely poor, thin on
content and rather hollow in production
quality. Obviously, the staging limitations
dictate how expansive one can be with
ideas, but Donal still managed to present
a story that flowed well, was decently
dressed and gave many individuals an
opportunity to shine. Most importantly, he
instilled in his cast a joy of performance
and an appreciation of the age-old story.
His cast certainly didn't let him down.
Opportunities for effective choreography
were few and far between, due to the
same restrictions, but choreographer,
Diarmuid O'Meara, did his best to give
the show some form and shape with his
efforts. His choruses and principals did
what they could to execute their moves
effectively and efficiently.
The set for the show, necessarily, had
to be fairly basic in design, but the
pieces that were used were sufficient to
give a sense of location, and they were
nicely painted. Changes of scenery
were more than adequately handled by
Stage Manager, Ruth Garvey Williams
and team. Lighting, similarly, was simple
but effective, and the sound quality was
quite good, although some lines were
lost through late cueing. Costumes were
all good, bright and colourful, including
the nicely made mermaid costumes.
The Storyteller looked nicely elegant yet
mysterious with her long cape. Captain
Hook's hook was very effective. Make-up
was most satisfactory and hairstyles for
the central characters were appropriate.
In the title role of Peter, Patrick Gill showed
a good stage sense, a confident air and
a voice that, with development, should
become a fine instrument. Despite the
lack of inspiration given by those pesky
backing tracks, he did very well to keep
in time and tempo. He has the making of
a fine actor.
Caoimhe Murray, as Wendy Darling, had a
tendency to play everything out front, and
maybe needed to play more to those who
shared the stage with her. Her accent was
very good, as were her emotions, and her
good acting was complemented by a very
pleasing vocal quality.
Tia Cooper, as Captain Hook, worked hard
to put comedy into her lines and scenes,
and managed well in establishing herself
as the bad guy of the piece. Her singing
was fine for the demands of the role.
Very much holding the whole show
together
was
the
Storyteller,
very
effectively played by Sheila Brown. As a
good narrator should, she had a melodic
voice and very good expression. Spoiler
alert - She also turns out to be Wendy as
an old woman, and she played that scene
particularly well. Her vocal quality was
also extremely secure.
As Wendy's younger brothers, Domhnall
Doherty as John and Lee McLaughlin as
Michael gave good account of themselves,
with some nice sincere moments and
good comical touches.
Brendan Fletcher was a very amusing and
well played Mr Darling, extracting much
silliness from the role, while his long-
suffering wife, Mrs. Darling, was played
with a mellower tone by Maria Fitzpatrick,
who perhaps needed to put more facial
expression into her vocal efforts, which
were most pleasant.
Maria Doherty-Lee gave a good account
of herself as house-maid, Liza.
Sean Tolley made a big impact playing
the comically nasty Smee, milking his
business to the full and making worthy
vocal contributions alongside Hook.
The silent but delightful Lily May Tolley
gave
fine
expression
and
graceful
elegance to her mime role as Tinkerbell.
Cassie McKinney created a very likeable
character with Tiger Lily, making a very
good job of her first principal role, and
Tommy Doherty looked well and had a lot
of fun playing Nana the dog.
With limited space, there weren't many
opportunities for the choruses to exhibit
their potential as dancers, but they did all
that was asked of them with enthusiasm.
They were vocally secure and well-turned
out. There were a few uncredited soloists
within their ranks who sang extremely
well, and overall, they all made a valuable
contribution to the show.
Good work went into preparing the cast
onstage for their vocal work, in the hands
of MD, Aoife Lennon and vocal coach,
Louise Crossan, and I must commend
them, as well as the performers, on doing
as well as they did, working with and
singing against such poor-quality backing
tracks. The principals displayed some
very pleasing vocal quality, and choral
harmonies were in evidence.
Much as St Mary's Hall has history and
character, I was left feeling that, given the
talent available, and the good efforts of
the production team, live musicians and
a venue that allowed for more expansive
creativity would have made this a much
more flamboyant presentation. As it was,
I'm extremely grateful to all concerned
for making my journey to the far North an
enjoyable and worthwhile experience.,

It's not at all surprising that when you
combine the dark fairytales of the Brothers
Grimm, and the musical theatre geniuses
of Stephen Sondheim and James Lapine,
that you come up with the fascinating,
charming
and
extremely
challenging
musical that is Into The Woods.
Filled with an array of diverse and colourful
characters, inspired lyrics and wonderful
music, it really has so much to offer any
ambitious society, and Maynooth have
tackled it with energy, creativity and a high
level of talent.
The set, by John O'Donoghue, was
artistically beautiful, comprised of off-
white tree trunks, ramps, and full or
broken gilt-edged picture frames, which
were beautifully used at the beginning
and end of the show to highlight the main
characters of the story. The effect was
quite stunning, but wouldn't have been
half so effective had it not been brilliantly
lit. Colourful beams of light, brighter pools
of light, eerie effects and atmospheres
were wonderfully created by the lighting
team. The overall combination of set and
lights was close to perfection. Apart from
one of two late cues with mics, the quality
of sound was very good indeed, including
the many sound effects. Stage Manager,
Olivia Parkinson-Coombs, had her crew
and the cast very well prepared for the
movement of scenery, all of which was
achieved with minimum fuss.
Director, Emma Thornton, did a wonderful
job of pulling together these technical
elements and a strong and willing
cast to present a smooth production
that had pace and energy from start
to finish. She realised the comedy of
the piece as much as the tragedy and
used the stage space beautifully to
create atmosphere and fluency in the
performance.
Those
large,
weather-
beaten, picture frames that dominated
the set were not only like snapshots of
the main characters, but represented
the homes of those characters, from
whence they began their journeys, and to
where they returned for the finale. Such
touches, and a good realisation of the
personality of each character, displayed
a very good understanding of the whole
piece. This was beautiful work, and while
choreography isn't a major feature of the
show, there was enough interesting and
varied movement to enhance the overall
presentation.
That the company were meticulously
rehearsed in their rhythmically challenging
musical pieces, with good emphasis on
diction-clear performance of the very
tricky lyrics, was evident throughout the
show, and is a credit to Musical Director,
Ben Cully. Conductor, Celine Leong,
was fortunate to have a pit filled with
accomplished musicians, and she led
them with security. Only once or twice
was there a hesitation between musical
pieces that saw a principal or two looking
to her for an intro, but no one was ever
lost or fell behind the beat. Principal
vocals were remarkably good, sometimes
breath-taking. The clarity of diction and
the fluency of rhythm in the "Your Fault"
number was a highlight of precision and
musical ability.
Seán MacMathúna, as The Baker, played
his role with confidence and charm, always
expressing the right emotions through his
voice and his body language. His control
of the difficult rhythms and lyrics was
flawless and his vocal quality was never
in question. An excellent performance.
As his wife, Ellie-Anne Smith, there was
warmth and sincerity in her portrayal,
combined with a strong sense of comedy,
and again, a most pleasing vocal quality.
Together, they made a very natural and
realistic married couple, very much in love
but also very capable of exasperating
each other.
Enda Keating started hesitantly in the
role of Jack, but soon settled into a very
fine performance, divinely comical in his
simplicity, and well able for the demands
of the script and score. Jack's Mother
was played delightfully by Louise Gilmore,
displaying good character and timing and
a very pleasant voice.
Alison Kiernan Whelan brought excellent
vocal and facial comedy to the character
of the carefree and impetus child, Little
Red, showing no fear at all of the threats
to her existence. She grew in stature as
the story progressed and gave life and
energy to her vocals.
Anna Bergin, as The Witch, knocked
the ball out of the park with her superb
vocal range and quality. As well as
playing her character with venom, verve
and a delightful confusion of conflicting
emotions, her singing was passionate,
powerful,
spine-tingling
and
quite
awesome.
Grace Nolan brought a sincerity and, dare
I say it, grace… to the role of Cinderella,
beautifully capturing the passion of
a dreamer and contrasting it with the
disillusionment of a realist. A thoughtful
and enchanting performance with a
mellow and beautiful vocal quality.
Cinderella's Prince and Rapunzel's Prince,
comically portrayed by Harry Kingsland
and Conor McNamee, oozed with shallow
charm, vacant intellect, and a sad but
hilarious desire to outdo each other in their
fake heartache, with a brilliantly performed
Agony. Harry Kingsland's seduction scene
with the Baker's wife was comedy gold.
The Narrator, played by James Sheridan,
was smooth, suave and quite frankly,
annoyingly handsome, so I was delighted
when he was sacrificed to the giant! (Very
nicely played though!)
Cinderella's Step Mother was portrayed
as a heartless, scheming social-climber,
with a voice that would disturb the dead,
by a very talented Colleen Doyle, whose
facial expressions and body language
were complementary to her strong vocal
ability. Her obnoxious daughters Lucinda
and Florinda, were played with great visual
and vocal comedy by Eimear Molloy and
Molly Wilson, both of whom excelled at
playing their blind scenes.
Rapunzel, a slightly underwritten part, was
still strongly portrayed by a very tuneful
and mellow Ella Burke. The Mysterious
Man, reminiscent of a hobbit, was played
with quirky charm by Lar Bathe, who also
played the revelation of being the Baker's
father with sincerity. Dan Lavelle was a
sleazy, scary wolf, with a good sense of
comedic timing, and Ainé Fox, gave a
warm character to Little Red's Granny.
That poor emaciated Milky Cow was
brought to life with good expression and
reactions by Emily Little. Brandon Byrne
was a suitably obnoxious and uncaring
Steward, and good support came from
Catherine
Gallagher
as
Cinderella's
mother.
Birds, trees, woodland spirits, and scenery
shifters were all very capably played by an
industrious ensemble, consisting of Joe
Keane, Joey Crinion, Aoife Daly, Grace
Hanan, Niamh Ready, Megan Byrne,
Becky Casley and Rubimae Hoskins, all
of whom added good movement, great
vocals and a strong presence to all their
scenes.
Much work was done on a fine selection
of very good wigs for the ladies, and some
of the men, but especially The Witch and
Rapunzel. The Witch's make-up, before
she transformed was gruesome and very
well done. The Wolf and the Mysterious
Man were well created. The step-sisters
were suitably gawdy. Costumes too,
were well-selected and everyone looked
comfortable in their attire. The addition of
twigs, leaves and feathers to the ensemble
outfits was enough to suggest their
function and role in the story. The massive
boot of the Female Giant was very good,
as was the body of Milky White. Other
props were very good and appropriate,
and not just on stage either. A beautiful
3D model of the set was on display in the
foyer of the venue, and one entered the
auditorium through tree lined passages, in
the same style as the set, and there was a
quaint wooded area, with a picture frame,
that was by-passed on the way to your
seats. These features beautifully drew the
audience into the atmosphere even before
the show began.
With such a thorough and successful
production, their legacy, as students, is
the standard they have set for those who
come after them to emulate. Thank you
all, for a truly beautiful production and a
wonderful night of entertainment.

Crazy For You, like similar shows in the
same genre, (Singing in the Rain, 42nd.
Street) cries out for the spectacle and
sparkle of an Opera house or an expansive
major theatre venue, but even if it
becomes a more homely show, translated
into the confined setting of a stage such
as the one in St Mary's Secondary School,
in Baldoyle, it has a good enough script,
great comedy and well-painted characters
for it to make an impact.
The set for this particular production was
of a decent quality, and quite functional,
using curtains and a few theatre signs to
depict New York, and trucks to represent
the Deadrock township. Perhaps the
painting of these could have been a bit
tidier, but they were decent enough to
suggest location. These were rotated and
positioned efficiently by the stage crew,
under the guidance of stage manager, Matt
Keena. There was also a nice projected
interior of the theatre image, and perhaps
there were opportunities to project even
more, to add more variety. Props and
furniture were good and era appropriate.
There were only minor problems with
lighting,
with
principals
occasionally
moving through dark shadows, but by and
large, good atmospheres were created.
Sound quality was very good and well
balanced.
The pace at the start of the show was a
little laid back, but once things got going,
the action fairly rattled along, and director,
Nina O'Keeffe, used the stage space very
well for creating nice pictures. Characters
were well defined, and the accent on
the comedy of the piece was very good.
The mirrored scene between Bobby and
Zangler was well directed, while some of
the other comedy could have been a little
more pointed, but generally, everything
ran very smoothly. The mock fight scenes
between the cowboys, while lacking the
space to break up furniture and to have
cowboys collapsing through balconies,
was still nicely handled.
Choreographer,
Sinéad
McCrohan,
produced
good,
lively
and
varied
routines that were pitched at a level that
allowed the chorus and dancers to show
themselves in a very good light. There
was nice work done, also, with Bobby and
Polly in their duets. Slap That Bass and
I've Got Rhythm were the highlights, with
ever changing patterns and styles and
great company involvement. The Follies
made the most of their routines too, and
between them and the townsfolk, they
added colour, atmosphere to all their
scenes, constantly involved and reacting
well to the focal point of the action. They
also produced good vocal harmonies,
particularly in I've Got Rhythm and Stiff
Upper Lip.
An
extremely
well-played
overture
highlighted the abundant talent of the
orchestra and the confident leadership of
Musical Director, Carmel Whelan, and it
was great to hear the wonderful musical
score played so competently. The Double
Bass solos during Slap That Bass were
particularly impressive. The small number
of men in the chorus left the men-only
numbers a bit vocally fragile, but there
was good evidence of well-rehearsed
harmonies, which were particularly robust
when the whole company were involved.
Principals, similarly, were well-rehearsed
and secure in their vocal contributions.
Tempi and tone throughout the show
were delightfully smooth, and the balance
between pit and stage was very good.
Morgan Moore, in the role of Bobby, got the
show off to a fine start with good character,
good comedy and very capable song and
dance skills, with which he continued to
impress throughout the show. He made
good contrast between his Bobby and
his impersonation of Zangler, played his
romance with Polly very convincingly, and
created a highly likeable leading man, with
a tuneful crooning voice.
Karen McCourt, as Polly, was fiery and
vibrant in her interpretation, relaxed
and dismissive of unwanted attention,
delightful in her romantic encounters,
very capable in her comedy, and very
successful in her vocal contributions. This
was a lovely performance.
Karl Hoffman gave a nicely over-the-top
characterisation to Zangler, very theatrical
and demonstrative in his mannerisms, and
with a fine accent. His playing of the drunk
scene, and his haziness in the morning
after scene were displays of very good
comedy.
Kate Headon was an impressive Irene,
and played annoyingly enough to merit
rejection by Bobby. Secure in her comedy,
she delivered 'Naughty Baby' like a
seasoned dominatrix!
The role of Lank, normally played as a
thick, brutish thug, was given a more
whinging, spineless interpretation by
Robin Murray, which worked quite well,
and was full of animated angst at always
being the loser. His comedic timing was
good.
Lottie, mother of Bobby, was delightfully
played as demur and dismissive by
Colette O'Beirne, succeeding particularly
in her comical bitchiness towards Irene.
James O'Keeffe's Everett was placid and
confused, constantly lost in a nostalgic
trance, and very nicely played. Tess was
played with confidence and comedy
by Ceri McEvoy, flirtatious but totally in
control of her situation, while there was
a lovely ditzy, disziness about Nicola
Smith's Patsy. These two fronted the
Follies group extremely well, with Caoimhe
Henry, Gillian Hogan, Kate Canavan, Katie
Burrows, Rachel Morrissey and Sinead
McMullan giving good vocal and dance
support as the showgirls.
Ben O'Keeffe and Kathryn Gibbons as
Eugene and Patricia Fodor, provided a
good English quirkiness to the story, as
the eccentric, smart-stepping, guide-
writers, adding frivolous fun to their Stiff
Upper Lip number.
Heading up the assortment of local yokels
was Peter Fitzsimons as the gentle giant,
Moose, played with quaint simplicity, and
accompanied by Nathan Durkin's Mingo,
Jack Wright's Sam, Pat O'Keeffe's Pete,
Paul McCormack's Junior, and Aaron
Donnolly's Jimmy, all of whom added
nice harmonies, plenty of character and
good comedic action in their mock-fight
scenes.
The show was nicely costumed, with
attractive and colourful outfits for the
Follies routines, even if we did miss the
more flamboyant feathers and sequins
that are commonly associated with show-
girl routines. There were good hick-style
'out-west' outfits for the townsfolk. There
were nice sophisticated gowns on Irene
and Lottie, as befitted their characters
and indeed, all the principals were very
well turned out. Hairstyles were good for
the ladies, and make-up looked natural,
with a tad more showiness for the follies
than the townsfolk. All in all, the show was
visually pleasing.
I very much appreciated the warm
welcome to the show, and the hospitality
afforded me by a friendly and efficient
front of house staff. Thank you to all
concerned for a most entertaining evening
in the company of a talented, energetic
and enthusiastic society.

This was a very enjoyable and pleasing
production
by
Director,
Rebecca
Thompson, that saw principals with well-
defined characterisations, and moving
fluidly around the stage. Nice pictures
were created, and the choreography,
which mainly involved the children, was
apt and well-disciplined. The main set for
the show looked opulent and very well
constructed, and the side pieces served
well for both the mansion and the abbey,
but it would have been nice if the large
windowed piece at the back and the
carpeted stairway could have somehow
been covered for the terrace and outdoor
scenes. The projected scene of the
mountains at the start was very effective.
As far as the action was concerned, there
was a good flow to the production, and
what changes of scenery there were,
were well-handled by the crew, under
stage manager, Laura Douglas. Lighting
was colourful and effective at creating
atmosphere but a little more time needed
to be spent on ensuring that all areas of
the stage were sufficiently lit. The front
corners were frequently used for action
but were mostly in shadow. The sound
quality throughout the show was most
satisfactory.
This was also a nicely dressed show,
from the military uniforms of the adults
to the uniforms of the children, and their
colourful play clothes. Elsa was extremely
elegant
and
Max
was
casual
but
sophisticated in attire. Nuns outfits were
fine, except for varying lengths of robes
on the postulants. The Reverent Mother
had a beautiful cloak for the wedding
scene. Make-up was suitably subdued.
Props and dressing for the stage were fine
throughout.
I was quite captivated by Anna Gallagher's
Maria Rainer. This was a performance
that had good emotion, plenty of spirit
and assured vocals and movement
throughout. She carried herself well on
the stage, and built a strong relationship
with the Von Trapp children. Her forceful
reckoning with the Captain was very
nicely played, even if she had a slight
tendency to shout, and while I loved the
way her character developed beautifully
through the story, her romantic scenes
with the Captain could have been a tad
more believable.
Likewise, Mark Leonard, as Captain Von
Trapp, gave a strong and convincing
performance, moving from the strict
disciplinarian of a grieving widower to a
warmer and more receptive gentleman
under the influence of Maria's charm, and
his only weakness was the realisation of
his romantic encounters. He performed
his musical pieces most effectively.
Andrea Logue was deliciously superior in
the role of Elsa, making the most of the
comedy of her encounters with Maria, and
trying in vain to win the affections of the
Captain. Alongside her was a very capable
Uncle Max, played by Ronan Drummond,
with just the right amount of wit, charm
and underhanded mischief. His dealings
with the children were good and relaxed.
Clare Bradley's Mother Abbess, clearly
received her holy orders in Ireland and
never lost her accent in moving to Austria.
She played her role with wit and wisdom
and good sincerity in her religiosity.
She put good emotion into Climb Every
Mountain. She was ably supported in
her religious duties by Caroline Baker as
Sister Berthe, Rebecca Thompson as
Sister Margaretta and Sarah-Jane Mullen
as Sister Sophia, all of whom had good
individuality and performed How Do You
Solve A Problem very effectively.
Liesl Von Trapp was nicely portrayed by
Molly Phelan, who sang Sixteen Going On
Seventeen very well, danced delightfully,
and had a warm flirting relationship with
Rolf. She also played her later scenes with
good emotion. Rolf, very strongly played
by James Thompson, was courageous in
his courtship of Liesl, suitably intimidated
by the Captain and convincingly nastier
when he donned the swastika. He,
likewise, performed Sixteen Going on
Seventeen was commendably.
The rest of the Von Trapp children were
led by a confident Matthew Devenney as
Friedrich, a playful Erin Dolan as Louisa,
a kind-hearted Ethan Barron as Kurt, an
intuitive Brigitta played by Amelia Raw,
a shy and enchanting Marta played by
Pippa Kelly and a cute and adorable
Gretl played by Freya Kelly. They were all
extremely good in their various routines
and worked hard at their vocal harmonies.
Caolan Kelly was a capable and convincing
turncoat as Franz, while Donna Ponsonby
was a loyal and reliable house-keeper as
Frau Schmidt. Joe Harley's Herr Zeller was
quiet but menacing, and Gary McHugh
was more mannerly but still commanding
as Admiral Von Schriber.
With a mostly youthful chorus of nuns
and postulants, their vocal contributions
were valiant but a little thin, but they
compensated by being good in their
behaviour and their presentation, doing
all that was required of them. The adults
who danced at the party performed
comfortably, and the Nazi soldiers were,
as required, intimidating.
The children and other principals seemed
to have been well-tutored in their
harmonies, and while the nun's choruses
were a little thin, due to youthfulness,
there was evidence of good work on their
harmony from Musical Director, Gerard
Bradley. He also led a nice orchestra, who
provided a sympathetic accompaniment
to the vocalists on stage. A better 'organ'
voice on the keyboards might have
enhanced the Wedding processional, but
otherwise the music was very well played.
I can only imagine that some principal
songs were cut to reduce the running time
of the show, but I did miss "How Can Love
Survive" as it adds another dimension to
the characters of Elsa and Max.
Every time I see this show, it warms my
heart with memories of playing Kurt,
alongside my father, as Uncle Max, which
is why I love it very dearly. I'm quite sure
that every child who has played a young
Von Trapp, has experienced that feeling
of awe when they first march forward and
present themselves to the audience. This
production brought back that sense of awe
back to me. Thank you to all concerned
for a very pleasant evening of nostalgia
and heart-warming entertainment.

All Shook Up, at its core, is a comedic romp
of a juke-box musical, combining wit and
popular music to present entertainment
for entertainments sake. It doesn't attempt
to be deep, dark or intellectual, and
while it touches on topics like class/race
prejudice and gender stereotypes, it does
so with tongue firmly in cheek. It's really all
about fun and energy, and in this particular
production, it was the choreography that
was undoubtedly at the core of the energy.
Choreographer, Dylan O'Keeffe, created
many fast-moving, varied and exciting
routines, which the dancers seemed to
thoroughly enjoy performing. Sharper
finishing pictures would have prolonged
the applause at the end of each number,
but that's a minor point. Along with the
vibrant chorus numbers, there was good
work too on Devil in Disguise, A Little Less
Conversation and the Teddy Bear/Hound
Dog mix.
The ensemble, led by a highly confident
and competent Dance Captain in Rachel
Fox, performed all their routines with high
levels of energy and enthusiasm. While
some of the vocal choruses seemed a
little thin and a little ragged, there were
some moments of fine singing and good
harmony, but it was definitely in the good
and precise execution of their dance
numbers that they excelled.
Eoghan O'Leary, as Chad, had good
charm and swagger for the role, and a
very decent crooner voice. Some of his
comedy was a little underplayed, and he
occasionally got a little tongue-tied in his
dialogue, but he was consistently good
and very likeable.
Caoimhe Keane got the character of
Natalie just right, and did a good job of
realising the comedy, especially when
transformed into Ed. Some of her delivery
was a little rushed, and with a little more
confidence, she will let her abilities shine
more brightly. She sang her numbers with
good expression.
Fergal Crowley gave a good nerdy quality
to Dennis, secure in his script and his
vocals, and extremely likeable as the
underdog. I'd have been inclined to
exaggerate his awkwardness even more
to fully capitalise on his comedic potential,
but this was a very good performance
none-the-less.
Dara Keane gave a very good, solid
performance as Jim Haller, believable
as Natalie's father, and with a good
awkwardness about his feelings for Miss
Sandra. He sang and looked great in the
role, but more could have been made of
his comedic attempts to be young and
cool again.
Lorraine
was
played
with
youthful
enthusiasm and plenty of energy by Zoe
Allman Walsh, nicely establishing her
character and creating a good partnership
with Dean. Her vocals were also very
acceptable.
Cian Sprague was excellent as Dean Hyde,
capturing the innocence and the sense of
adventure of a youth rebelling against an
over-protective mother, and doing so with
fine voice and secure comedy.
Caoimhe Dunne was a vivacious Miss
Sandra, who played her passion at a
high level and injected it was plenty of
comedic touches. While her vocals were
a tad unpredictable, her character was
excellent and this carried her through to a
very fine performance.
Matilda was very comfortably portrayed
by Sarah Cleary, capturing the pious
attitude of the over-bearing Mayor and
mother. Devil in Disguise was very well
performed.
Conor Walsh, as Earl, made the most of
his opportunities, both in his silent mimed
existence, and especially when he found
his voice and his rhythm. His enthusiasm
during Burning Love was excellent and
quite hilarious.
The visual presentation of the show was
pleasing, with a good selection of era
appropriate costumes that suited the
characters, and hair and make-up that
was most satisfactory. There were some
good eye-catching outfits for the chorus
and dancers for numbers such as Devil in
Disguise and A Little Less Conversation,
and the wedding dresses for the principal
ladies were quite fetching.
I think that Director, Matt Palliser-Kehoe,
perhaps took the story a little too seriously,
and maybe needed a lighter touch in
handling the comedy of the piece. While
there were nice moments of affection,
there was much vocal and visual humour
that wasn't fully realised.
For me, however, the aspect of the
show that created most problems was
the technical presentation. Despite the
best efforts of Stage Manager, Máirtin
Ó'Cathasaigh, and his team, there simply
wasn't enough of a set to provide colour
and atmosphere to the production. There
were plenty of moving lights, and some
nice effects, but the lighting plot lacked
focus, with much dialogue played in
shadow, The sound system was good
though.
Musically, the show was a bit of a mixed
bag, with some fine chorus singing and
some secure principals, while others
seemed to have some pitch issues, that
weren't helped by a slightly insecure
performance
from
the
musicians.
Musical Director, Lucia Schmetterer, and
Conductor, Rachel Rentz, had clearly
done good work in the rehearsals, but
there was an uncertainty about the musical
performance that perhaps needed more
leadership or discipline.
Despite the criticisms, I enjoyed the energy
and enthusiasm of this young company.
I deeply appreciate the work and effort
that goes into putting on any show, and
even when ideas don't always come
together perfectly, that doesn't diminish
my admiration of commitment and good
intentions. Like most in the audience, I left
the theatre well-entertained and humming
the great tunes. My sincere thanks to all
concerned for the warm hospitality.

The Addams Family certainly has been a
popular show this season, so it's just as
well it's a show I don't mind seeing time
after time. This was another clean and well-
delivered rendition, with good emphasis
on all the right areas of the production.
Director, Sean Power, elicited good and
secure performances from his cast, and
ensured that they were presented in front
of an eye-catching and well-constructed
set. The early pace of the dialogue was a
tad slow to get going, but once it settled
into its stride, it fairly rattled along. A very
nicely designed and painted set made a
strong impact from the start of the show
and was enhanced in various scenes with
good visual props. The gates were a nice
centre piece and the black cloth made for
a good UV lighting effect for the Moon
number. The stage crew, led by Mary
Heaney, did a good job of keeping things
running smoothly. Lighting, generally was
good and very atmospheric, but it must
be noted that if specials are being used,
principal characters need to be in the
right place for them to be effective. Sound
quality was of a very good standard.
Some of the comedy was a tad
telegraphed in delivery, but there were
also some lovely original touches, Lurch's
crying being a highlight.
Another
highlight
was
the
visual
presentation of the show, with an excellent
set of costumes, particularly for the chorus
of ancestors, enhanced by excellent
make-up and a mad assortment of wigs.
They all blended together perfectly with
the beautiful set.
The orchestra, under Musical Director,
Finola Higgins, played the score with great
energy and with good consistent tempi
throughout. They were nicely balanced
and sympathetic to the vocalists on stage.
There were also good harmonies coming
from the chorus and mostly secure vocals
from the principal line, in what was
obviously a well-rehearsed show. Finola
conducted the show with a light touch
and a certain Joie de vivre.
David Cooke was a very secure and
polished Gomez Addams, with a good
accent and an easy listening vocal quality.
While his comedy was good, he tended
to telegraph his punchlines a little, where
perhaps they could have been a tad more
off-the-cuff. Nevertheless, this was a
confident and enjoyable performance.
Gráinne Caldbeck was a vivacious and
volatile Morticia, looking perfect for
the role and possessing a strong and
expressive voice. Her comedy, if a little
more animated than one might expect
from her role, was well timed and well
delivered. Her stubborn relationship with
Gomez was very well crafted.
Laoise Flanagan made a strong impression
as Wednesday, sharing her mother's
volatility
and
displaying
Dominatrix
tendencies towards her brother and her
boyfriend. Her vocals were very good,
and her sentiments were always strongly
expressed. There was lovely sincerity in
her scenes with her father.
Adam Lavin was a wonderful Pugsley,
disturbingly alternative and individual in
his masochistic tendencies, but equally
genuine in his close bond with his sister.
He got good comedy from his script and
from his facial reactions, and his vocal
performance was very reliable. Very well
done.
Kieran Croghan brought great comedy out
of Uncle Fester, with excellent timing and
delivery, both physically and verbally. As
the narrator of sorts, he worked a good
relationship with the audience and as a
romantic, his affection for the moon was
delightfully silly. Nicely played.
Michéal Kilheeney made a strong impact
in the role of Lurch, grunting his way
delightfully into the audience's hearts. His
crying scene when Morticia was departing
was comedy gold. He maintained his slow
and deliberate walk perfectly throughout.
Good singing in the finale too.
There
was
a
good,
self-assured
performance of Lucas Beineke by Conor
Walsh, standing up to his parents and
falling under the spell of Wednesday.
Strong in his vocals and secure in his
comedy, he pitched this role at just the
right level.
As his father, Mal Beineke, Pat Walsh
came across as a very realistic stubborn
father, impatient with his wayward son,
and somewhat oblivious of his wife's
desires. Pat achieved the stuffiness of
the early scenes most amusingly, and
blossomed into his more youthful self
with good comedic effect as the story
unfolded.
Performance of the night came from Janet
Feeney as Alice Beineke, at first potty and
poetic, and ultimately frenetic and fiery
with unleashed passion. In both guises,
her delivery was excellent and hilarious,
and she let rip with a well-delivered
Waiting during Full Disclosure.
Adding further chaos and craziness to the
story was Majella Flanagan's demented
Grandma, played with a strong dose of
comedy and caricature.
While there aren't that many opportunities
for big, choreographed numbers in
this
show,
those
that
did
present
themselves were very nicely created by
Choreographer Ria Purcell, and nicely
executed by the company. The Moon and
Me perhaps needed a little more magic,
and while the Tango was well performed
by Morticia and Gomez, a fuller chorus
might have enhanced it even more. The
Chorus of deceased ancestors made a
visually stimulating contribution to the
action, comically animated and excellent
in dress and make-up. They moved well
when the opportunities arose and made a
worthy effort with their vocal prowess.
Regardless of fairly minor hiccups, this
was still a splendid and highly entertaining
production, and I thank you all for a very
enjoyable night in the company of the
Addams Family.

There's nothing like a bit of gospel music
to raise your spirits, and with a stream
of fabulous numbers, from "Raise Your
Voice" to "Take Me To Heaven" to "Spread
The Love Around", Sister Act has to the
material to fill one with an elevated sense
of well-being, and when it's as well-
presented as this Lisnagarvey offering, it's
an absolute tonic. Director, Wilfie Pyper,
ensured that the pace of this production
was perfectly pitched. The dialogue was
racy, the scene changes were smooth,
the comedy was well-timed and from
curtain up to curtain down, the show ran
like a well-oiled machine. A very well-
dressed stage was nicely used, with
good pictures when the chorus weren't
engaged in movement. Principal action
was well-directed and characters were
well-realised.
The highlights of the set design were
the scenes set within the Convent,
with beautifully painted stained-glass
windows, that were enhanced frequently
by very effective lighting. The other
scenes, played against roll-on flats, were
straightforward but well painted and they
worked effectively. Stage Management,
under Andrew Bell, ensured that scene
changes were slick and smooth. There
were so many good lighting effects
that it pains me to say that sometimes
the basic key lighting was not up to the
same standard. There has been a trend
with shows I have seen recently to flood
the stage with moving lights, gobos and
all manner of effects, without having
ensured that the key lighting was securely
in place. There were several times in this
production when swirling lights created
beautiful patterns, but the soloists were
lost in shadows until a follow spot moved
to them, and other times when the focal
point was too dimly lit to balance against
strong back light. Among the very good
effects were good moving heads during
the up-beat numbers and very strong
finishing pictures for songs.
Musical Director, Keith Pyper, had a
very strong band of musicians, whose
excellent playing was marred only by a
tendency to be over-exuberant. All of the
principals were, on occasions, somewhat
overwhelmed by the pit, not through any
lack of musical ability, but through an
imbalance between pit and stage. When
the soloists were clearly heard, the vocal
quality was always there, and the chorus
had no problems being heard when they
were belting out their gospel harmonies.
The rhythm and the pace of the music was
always spot-on.
While dialogue was always clearly heard,
I felt that the sound operator needed to
boost some soloists when they were
singing against a full chorus, and perhaps
to try to balance better with the fulsome
orchestra sound.
As Deloris Van Cartier, Hannah Conlon
displayed a vocal prowess that was most
suitable for the role. She also had a very
good sense of comedy, and played her
playful romance with Eddie very nicely.
Sustaining a somewhat unusual accent
throughout, this was a strong and confident
performance. Both her "Fabulous Baby"
reprise and her "Sister Act" solo, were
very passionate and moving.
Wendy Pyper gave a touch of dignity
and refinement to the role of the Mother
Superior, excellent in her delivery of her
lines, well-tuned in to her comedy and
with a most pleasant and confident voice.
Her range of emotions was very well
displayed during "I Haven't Got A Prayer."
Fiona Rice brought good charm and
sincerity to the role of Sister Mary Robert,
delightfully shy early on and growing in
confidence to a well-delivered "The Life I
Never Led".
Jane McKibbin turned in a wonderful
performance as Sister Mary Lazarus, fiery
and feisty at the outset and comically
'hip' as the story progresses. Her comedy
and her vocals were very strong. Equally
gutsy and spirited was Cate McQuade as
Sister Mary Patrick, delightfully zealous
in her religious fervor but also very game
for adventure. This was a well-realised
character.
Karen Hawthorne, as Tina, and Amy
Galashan, as Michelle, gave strong
performances
as
Deloris's
backing
vocalists and both danced as confidently
as they sang, adding a lot of sass to their
characters.
Sean Harkin as Eddie Souther, captured
the nervous energy of his character with
great effect, winning the sympathy of
the audience as he attempted to be a
hero to Deloris. This was a very strong
performance, displaying that Sean can be
as good at sentiment as he is at comedy,
and his comedy is excellent. Nicely sung
too.
Simon Pyper gave a nasty and sinister
performance as Curtis, just as the
character should be, and he was a good
natural leader of his gang. His vocals on
"When I Find My Baby" were menacing
and very nicely sung.
Tony Young made the most of his comedic
opportunities
as
Monsignor
O'Hara,
delightfully flippant in his dealings with the
Mother Superior, and robustly theatrical in
his appreciation of the new style of church
service. Very well played.
I loved the cheesy comedy of Jack
Cranston as Pablo, Joshua Martin as Joey
and Patrick Glover as TJ, both individually,
with their well-realised characterisations,
and collectively, in their brilliantly funny
"Lady in the Long Black Dress". They
displayed good vocals and harmonies
too.
Several of the chorus contributed to the
story in cameo roles, and did so with
confidence, and as a group, they were full
of energy and precise in their movement.
The big nun's chorus numbers were a
highlight of the show, well-danced, bright
and colourful and very well-sung. This
was a great team effort. A very good
job was done by choreographer, Jordan
Rosborough, on those choral numbers.
There was good variety in her moves and
plenty of energy from the performers. The
sequences with Deloris, Michelle and Tina
were also nicely devised, as was the very
funny "Lady in the Long Black Dress".
"Bless our Show" was also delightfully
quirky. All round, very nicely presented
choreography.
When the lighting and the set blended
perfectly to produce beautiful pictures on
the stage, these were richly enhanced by
excellent costuming. The variety of roll-
down front pieces on the nun's costumes
was quite superb, from the initial glitzy
addition to the normal habit, to the
multicolored set, to the sparkling finale
robes. The nuns also looked great in their
nightwear. The gangster's outfits were
perfect for the era, and I loved their prison
outfits in the final number. Sweaty Eddie's
quick changes onstage were super-
slick, and the Monsignor's outfits were
very good. Great work was also done on
wigs and hairstyles, and nothing was out
of order from a make-up point of view.
Overall, the show was visually excellent.
Despite those issues with the balance of
sound, and lighting, from a performance
point of view, this was a very polished
production, from a man who knows his
craft, and I am grateful to all concerned
for the hospitality, the high performance
levels, and for a wonderful evening of
joyous entertainment.

The first time I saw Legally Blonde, I was
irritated by its cheesy Americanisms,
"Oh My God you guys" rattled my brain
and those 'snaps' just irritated me,
(actually, they still do!) but I quickly grew
to appreciate how much the show had
to offer, with a highly amusing script,
great music and a wonderful variety of
characters. This production, by Striking
Productions of Carlow, affirmed my high
opinion of the show, and threw up some
very capable performances. With the
exception of a few temporary glitches, the
whole show ran smoothly on a set that,
while not over-elaborate, was clean, tidy
and functional.
The main set for the show was well-painted
and constructed and made a good impact
from the get-go. With a reversible door
centre-stage, it worked well as the Delta
Nu Sorority House and as the façade for
Harvard. Other scenes were reasonably
well created by using simple in-set flats,
the best of these being the lighted flats
for the Department store, which might
have been even better had they had more
dressing. Stage Management, under the
direction of Aileen Farrell, coped well with
the scene changes, and a good variety of
props, helped to create atmosphere in the
various scenes. Lighting was generally
very effective, with good use of colour
and well-aimed pools of area lighting.
The sound quality was very good and
very balanced throughout, excepting
the hiccup with Brooke's mic during the
skipping scene.
Director, Robert O'Neill, showed a good
eye for detail with this show, with sets,
costumes and lighting all working well
together in presenting a very smooth
and coordinated production. Characters
were well-realised, and the action of
the show flowed very naturally, with no
uncomfortable moves or disruptions to the
pace. The stage space was well utilised,
and entrances and exits made sense.
A very fine orchestra, situated behind the
main set, and under the direction of Joan
Butler, played the score with accuracy,
good tone and tempi throughout. The
good vocal harmonies, evident in all the
